items.title: How Ceuta and migration are defining Spain's snap election
items.content:
How Ceuta and migration are defining Spain's snap election
Submitted by
Olivia Hooper
on
Fri, 11/27/2026 - 16:08
While the vote was triggered by domestic paralysis, anti-migration sentiment has become a key campaign focus
Relatives and friends wait for the return of people who crossed into Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta, at Morocco’s Bab Sebta border crossing, on 2 August 2026 (Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP)
Off
Spain is heading into
snap elections
after a turbulent period defined by a severe housing crisis and tensions over migration, fuelled by an incident in which
70,000 migrants
from
Morocco
entered the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in late July.
Prime Minster Pedro Sanchez’s position became even more tenuous after Spain’s second fatal train crash of 2026, which
killed 69 people
in October, just a few weeks after the snap election announcement.
Ceuta has been
a dominating
factor on the campaign trail so far, with the migration crisis playing directly into the hands of the opposition parties.
The consensus is that Spain’s
conservative
People’s Party (PP) and the far-right Vox will likely form the country’s ruling coalition, together providing enough seats to secure a
176-seat parliamentary majority
. Polls suggest the PP could win about 130 seats, the Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) 110, and Vox 63.
Rather than starting his campaign in Madrid, PP leader
Alberto Nunez Feijoo
soft-launched in the enclave of Ceuta shortly after the snap election was announced. The move placed migration, border security and the future of Ceuta at the core of his political messaging.
The Spanish enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla are the European Union’s
only land borders
with Africa. Since the Ceuta incident, an unprecedented tragedy that caused
141 deaths
, Reuters estimated last month that around
10,000 migrants
remained in the enclave.
The current focus on Ceuta has overshadowed Spain’s domestic failures, namely its housing crisis. The PP and Vox recently joined forces to
vote against
emergency reforms aimed at protecting tenants, tabled after an 87-year-old woman,
who has since died
, was evicted from her home over unpaid rent.
Border rhetoric
Across Spain, evictions reportedly affect some
25,000
people annually. During a
general strike
this month, an estimated four million workers took to the streets to protest soaring rent costs and the national housing deficit.
But rather than focusing on these issues, Feijoo and Vox leader Santiago Abascal, like many right-wing western politicians, have opted to bolster their rhetoric on a hardline anti-immigration stance, presenting Ceuta as a test of the government’s ability to manage Spain’s external borders.
Feijoo has been open in blaming Rabat “for action or
omission
” in the migration incident. His stance starkly contrasts with the position of Sanchez, who has
repeatedly
said there is no evidence of any involvement by Morocco.
Feijoo as prime minister could risk freezing bilateral relations from day one if he arrives in Rabat leading with hardline policies and ultimatums
Abascal has been highly critical of Sanchez’s leadership on Ceuta,
dubbing
him “the candidate of Morocco”.
If elected, Feijoo maintains his
first trip
would be to Morocco to establish a “red line” with King Mohammed VI, ensuring that Spain’s “territorial integrity and sovereignty” is not compromised.
Yet despite the efforts of the far right to rally anti-immigration and wider anti-Morocco sentiment as a campaign weapon, the hardline posturing is inadvertently strengthening Rabat’s hand. Calls for troop deployments or harsher border
crackdowns in Ceuta
ignore the fact that security relies on Rabat’s cooperation.
This was evidenced in Ceuta. Spain
deployed its army
to help stabilise the border, and began to return tens of thousands of people. Such a large-scale operation, with more than
48,000 returned
in 24 hours, would not have been possible without the cooperation of Moroccan security forces.
By blaming Rabat for “action or omission”, Feijoo is effectively emphasising that Morocco has the upper hand on border security.
Bilateral relations
Amid the snap election theatrics, Morocco made its position clear at the opening of parliament on 9 October, when King Mohammed VI defended Rabat’s relationship with Spain. He also explicitly warned that Morocco would not be
influenced
by “pressure, threats or blackmail”.
“I wish to point out that this partnership is a sovereign choice and a voluntary commitment,” the king said.
His comments didn’t appear to sway Feijoo, who has remained steadfast in his border narrative. In an interview with
El Pais
published on 10 November, Feijoo was asked whether he feared reprisals from Morocco if he were to become prime minister.
Morocco's revived claim to Ceuta and Melilla is not a demand for decolonisation
Read More »
In response, Feijoo referred to the Ceuta incident as an “invasion” of Spain - a term he has used on
several
occasions - and vowed that if elected, he would tell Morocco that Spain would never invade its land, and ask for reciprocity.
“What I hope for is to restore confidence with Morocco and clarify who was behind this,” he said. “To know why the interior minister, the defence minister and the prime minister hid information from us.”
Feijoo added: “The two states must be allies and collaborators, because that benefits both sides. I am not an enemy of Morocco. Now, I won’t compromise on Spain’s territorial integrity.”
Three separate
opinion
polls published on 16 November weighed in the potential right-wing coalition’s favour, even though Sanchez’s PSOE managed to regain some popularity.
But pairing up Feijoo and the unrelenting Abascal would mean less flexibility when it comes to diplomatic talks on all important topics with Rabat, including border security.
Considering his abrasive tone, Feijoo as prime minister could risk freezing bilateral relations from day one if he arrives in Rabat leading with hardline policies and ultimatums - a far cry from Sanchez’s soft approach.

items.title: Saudi coalition reports Houthi ballistic missile launch towards kingdom’s south
items.content:
Saudi coalition reports Houthi ballistic missile launch towards kingdom’s south
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said its air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis toward the southern region of the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence briefly issued a warning alert over Khamis Mushait in the southwestern Asir province, before announcing that the threat had passed.
Yemeni government forces also shot down a Houthi drone over the eastern front of Taiz city, where fighting has continued, Al Jazeera reported.
Two people died in a drone attack on the northwest front of the city, the Taiz Siege Affairs Office announced.
The report said it was unclear if those deaths were the same as the three civilian deaths, including a child, reported earlier by Yemen's government-run Saba news agency in attacks in Taiz province.

items.content:
Monia Indge, 58, who has terminal cancer, escorted from supermarket after staff using FaceWatch technology misidentified her
A woman with terminal cancer has been left “traumatised and violated” after being falsely accused of shoplifting and banned from Sainsbury’s by staff using facial recognition technology.
Monia Indge, 58, was shopping with her husband in the Walters Yard branch of Sainsbury’s in Bromley on 7 November when she was suddenly told to leave by a member of staff who told her she was “banned for life” from the store.

South Africa accused of hypocrisy over Israeli offshore oil project
Submitted by
Azad Essa
on
Wed, 11/25/2026 - 20:09
South African activists say the government's approval of an Israeli company's offshore oil deal contradicts its climate commitments and legal action against Israel at the ICJ
South Africans rally in Sea Point, Cape Town, on 3 October 2026, ahead of the third anniversary of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza (Esa Alexander/Reuters)
Off
South African activists have accused the government of hypocrisy over its decision to approve an
Israeli
company's takeover of an offshore oil and gas project, saying the move undermines Pretoria's climate commitments and its case against Israel at the
International Court of Justice
(ICJ).
More than two months after Canada-based Eco Atlantic announced the transfer of its 37.5 percent stake in Block 1 CBK to Israel's Navitas Petroleum, activists say they are still waiting for a clear explanation from the government about why the deal was approved.
The offshore concession, transferred in September, is located in the Orange Basin, near South Africa's maritime border with Namibia. The basin stretches along the west coasts of both countries.
According to company estimates, the block could contain more than 3.6 billion barrels of prospective oil resources, attracting growing interest from international energy companies. Some have described the Orange Basin as "
Africa's Oil Frontier
".
One
publication
described the area under Navitas's control as "one of the most active exploration regions on the African continent".
But activists monitoring the deal say Pretoria's decision to approve Navitas's entry into the project threatens South Africa's marine environment and the livelihoods of coastal communities.
They also argue that the move contradicts South Africa's position at the ICJ, where it has accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza.
"Navitas is an Israeli fossil fuel company that materially benefits the Israeli economy," Tara Nair van Ryneveld of the Climate Justice Coalition told Middle East Eye.
"At a time when South Africa is pursuing international legal action concerning Israel's actions in Palestine, granting an Israeli company access to South Africa's petroleum resources raises serious questions about the consistency of our government's actions with its international obligations and stated foreign policy," van Ryneveld said.
Activists told MEE that environmental groups had raised concerns with the South African government about the proposed transaction months before Pretoria granted Navitas the necessary approvals.
'Granting an Israeli company access to South Africa's petroleum resources raises serious questions about the consistency of our government's actions'
-
Tara Nair van Ryneveld, Climate Justice Coalition
In an open letter to President Cyril Ramaphosa in June, the environmental justice organisation the Green Connection
called
on him to explain how the transaction aligned with South Africa's international human rights commitments, particularly as the country pursued its case against Israel at the ICJ.
As a signatory to the Paris Agreement, South Africa has also committed to reducing greenhouse gas emissions and transitioning towards a low-carbon, climate-resilient economy.
With the deal appearing imminent, a coalition of human rights and environmental organisations, including the South African BDS Coalition, Masifundise Development Trust, Natural Justice and the Climate Justice Coalition, wrote to Mineral and Petroleum Resources Minister Gwede Mantashe and the Petroleum Agency of South Africa (Pasa) in August, urging them to reject the transfer.
On 24 September, two days after Eco Atlantic announced that the deal had been completed, the groups
submitted
a request to Pasa under the Promotion of Access to Information Act, seeking records relating to the approval.
Activists say neither the presidency nor Pasa has responded to their concerns in the intervening months.
"This is ultimately about South Africa's credibility as a country that upholds international human rights law," a spokesperson for The Green Connection told MEE.
Contradictory government policy
Over the past three years, South Africa has been among the few countries willing to confront Israel over its genocidal war in Gaza.
In December 2023, Pretoria brought a case against Israel at the ICJ, accusing it of violating the Genocide Convention. More than 250,000 Palestinians have been killed or injured, while more than 80 percent of structures in Gaza have been damaged or destroyed.
Towards Palestinian Liberation: How resistance travels across borders
Read More »
Despite its actions at the ICJ, South Africa has continued to sell coal to Israel, even
increasing
exports and becoming the country's largest coal supplier during the genocide.
Pretoria has also
refused
to prosecute South African citizens who joined the Israeli military, despite national legislation prohibiting citizens from serving in a foreign country's armed forces without prior authorisation.
Moreover, the presidency has declined to sever diplomatic ties with Israel, despite a parliamentary vote
authorising
it to do so.
Activists say the decision to allow Navitas to acquire a stake in the offshore exploration block exposes a wider gap between Pretoria's position at the ICJ and its actions at home.
"The Navitas project contradicts efforts to sanction Israel for genocide and colonial expansion. It runs counter to what the United Nations has called for, which is the isolation of Israel," a spokesperson for South African Jews for a Free Palestine (SAJFP) told MEE.
The activists say they would have opposed exploration in the block regardless of the company involved, citing risks to South Africa's marine environment.
However, they argue that approving an Israeli company's involvement deepened their objections.
'The Navitas project contradicts efforts to sanction Israel for genocide and colonial expansion'
-
South African Jews for a Free Palestine spokesperson
"As offshore exploration sites pose a threat to South Africa’s coastal environments and communities, Zionism and the broader infrastructure of global extractive capitalism with which it is interdependent produces severe ecological harm everywhere," the spokesperson for SAJFP added.
Activists also argue that approving new oil and gas exploration runs counter to the urgent need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and limit global warming.
They say expanding exploration would encourage further fossil fuel production and deepen dependence on oil and gas at a time when South Africa should be moving towards cleaner energy sources.
In the Eastern Cape province, communities have waged a years-long legal battle against Shell's proposed offshore exploration along the Wild Coast.
In August, the Constitutional Court ruled against Shell and Impact Africa's oil exploration plans.
In its coverage of the legal victory against the multinational energy company, Greenpeace
said
the ruling "strengthens the case for African governments to move away from an economic dependence on fossil fuels and towards reliable renewable energy and green employment".
The myth of economic opportunity
Speaking at the South Africa-Namibia Bi-National Commission in July, Ramaphosa described the Orange Basin as "one of the world's most promising new energy frontiers".
The South African president said developing the basin could help build a regional energy industry spanning exploration, engineering, refining, petrochemicals, logistics, maritime services and advanced manufacturing.
Business leaders have also highlighted the prospects of investment, job creation and energy security in South Africa, where energy costs have soared.
But climate justice activists say they are sceptical of claims that ordinary South Africans would benefit from oil and gas extraction.
"This lack of transparency is deeply concerning, particularly when decisions of this scale have potentially irreversible consequences for our oceans, climate and coastal communities," van Ryneveld, from the Climate Justice Coalition, said.
Several activists pointed to academic studies suggesting that profits from offshore extraction tend to flow out of the country, leaving coastal communities to bear the environmental risks while receiving few lasting economic benefits.
'We should be investing in an energy transition that delivers lasting jobs and broader economic benefits without sacrificing our oceans or public finances'
-
The Green Connection
They said communities and small-scale fishers along the country's western coast were likely to be among those most affected, while benefiting the least.
"The oil and gas economy is structured in ways that concentrate and export wealth, while leaving governments and communities to bear the costs," Power Shift Africa, a Nairobi-based think tank working on climate and development policy, said in its May 2026 report: Pipe Dreams: How oil and gas fail to deliver economic development in Africa.
The report described oil and gas extraction as an "enclave economy", in which much of the equipment and services are imported while fuel and profits are largely exported.
It added that although the oil industry could account for a substantial share of a country's gross domestic product, it did not necessarily generate significant employment.
"Meanwhile, fishing and tourism already sustain tens of thousands of livelihoods that could be threatened by seismic surveys, oil spills and other operations," The Green Connection said.
"We need to look beyond the promise of investment and ask whether this is the best use of South Africa's natural resources. The evidence suggests that offshore oil and gas risks privatising the profits.
"We should be investing in an energy transition that delivers lasting jobs and broader economic benefits without sacrificing our oceans or public finances," The Green Connection added.
MEE reached out to Navitas for comment but did not receive a response by the time of publication.

items.content:
حوار - الصحافي الفرنسي فبريس أبغرال يحسم الجدل: "جوكوفيتش أعظم لاعب في رياضة التنس على مر العصور"
اعتبر الصحافي الرياضي الفرنسي فبريس أبغرال، وهو متخصص في رياضة التنس ويغطي كل أحداثها العالمية الكبرى منذ عدة سنوات، أن الصربي نوفاك جوكوفيتش هو "موضوعيا وتاريخيا" أفضل لاعب في هذه الرياضة. وقال في حوار لفرانس24 بمناسبة صدور كتابه "نوفاك جوكوفيتش هو الأعظم على مر العصور": "إحصائيا، هو الأعظم، فهو الوحيد الذي أحرز جميع الألقاب.. ويستوفي كل الشروط بلا استثناء".

items.title: Israeli strike killed two staff outside Gaza clinic, MSF says
items.content:
GENEVA, Nov 28 (Reuters) - Medical charity Médecins Sans Frontièreshas voiced outrage after an Israeli strike killed two of its staff outside a medical clinic in Gaza late on Friday.
"Our premises were clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military," it said. "We call for accountability."
Israel's military confirmed the strike but said the two MSF staff were "terrorists posing as humanitarian workers".

items.title: Unpaid TV licence or cycling on pavement could bar people from settling in UK
items.content:
Exclusive: New immigration rules will introduce strict threshold where any adult conviction triggers mandatory refusal
People could be barred from settling in the UK over minor infractions such as cycling on the pavement or failing to pay a TV licence, ministers have been warned before the introduction of new “earned settlement” rules.
Under the plans, which are to come into effect next year, securing indefinite leave to remain will become significantly harder for many people. The
rules
introduce a strict new threshold where any adult conviction resulting in a court disposal – including fines, community orders, conditional cautions, and absolute or conditional discharges – triggers mandatory refusal.

items.title: ‘I told it to never call me again’: AI bots wreak havoc with UK restaurant bookings
items.content:
Meta claims its Muse assistant will make users’ lives easier, but business owners say AI is driving them to go analogue
Restaurant owners are battling a horde of AI bots and returning to using the telephone instead of online booking as new virtual assistants launch in the UK – but sometimes even that isn’t enough to stop them.
This week, Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta launched its Muse AI assistant in the UK and is encouraging users to let it shop and make restaurant reservations. The bot is given access to the user’s email if they give it permission, and it can make restaurant bookings and go shopping on the user’s behalf.

items.title: Morning update
items.content:
Morning update
Good Morning Middle East Eye readers,
If you are just joining us, here are key developments from across the region and beyond:
*Two oil tankers have exploded and caught fire after striking mines near Oman's Khasab port and in the eastern part of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said.
*The US Central Command has said it forces disabled a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman after its crew allegedly attempted to evade the US naval blockade on Iran on Friday.
*The drone used in the attack on Kuwait that killed two Italians was manufactured in Iran, Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani has said.
*Two employees of Doctors Without Borders (MSF) were killed in an Israeli strike on one of the organisation's clinics in the Gaza Strip on Friday.
*Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have stressed the need for continuing joint efforts to support the "political and defence tracks" of the Mecca Defence Alliance, Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman said.
*Colonel Majed al-Nuzaili, spokesman for Yemen’s government forces, claimed as many as 726 attacks had been carried against Houthi positions over the past 24 hours.
*Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has rejected a new request from military chief of staff Eyal Zamir to authorise administrative detention orders against Israeli settlers involved in attacks against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, Kan reported.
*Houthi attacks in Yemen's Taiz province killed three civilians, including a child, according to the government-run Saba news agency.
*Saudi Arabia’s air defences have intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile launched by Yemen’s Houthis towards Riyadh, Major General Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition forces, said on X.
*UN special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory, Francesca Albanese, says Costa Rican immigration police are refusing to release her from an airport despite a Constitutional Court order allowing her to go to a hotel.
*Israeli police have detained Mel Duncan, co-founder of Unarmed Civilian Protection in Palestine (UCPiP), as he was returning to Tel Aviv after a tour of the occupied West Bank, the organisation said in a statement on X.
*Israeli jets have carried out a two-wave air raid on the town of Kfar Tibnit in southern Lebanon’s Nabatieh district, according to the country’s National News Agency.

Iranian tennis player Ali Yazdani has withdrawn from the men’s doubles quarterfinals of the ITF World Tennis Tour in Antalya, Turkey, to avoid playing an opponent from Israel, according to Irna.
Yazdani and his Russian partner Egor Khotchenkov were considered the leading contenders for the doubles title. They were scheduled to face an Austrian-Israeli pair in the quarterfinals on Friday.

items.title: Iran's flogging of singer was warning from anxious hardliners, insiders say
items.content:
By Parisa Hafezi, Emily Giles and Melory Ghazi
DUBAI, Nov 28 (Reuters) - Iran's flogging of a female singer this week for offending public decency was a display of force by an embattled clerical elite straining to uphold public obedience it once took for granted, Iranian insiders say.
Parastoo Ahmadi, 29, and four members of her production team received 74 lashes each on Monday for a livestreamed performance in a caravanserai near the holy Shi'ite Muslim city of Qom in which she had bare shoulders, no headscarf and male musicians, defying Iran's theocratic legal code.

items.title: 'Banana republic again': Former Costa Rican president slams Albanese ban
items.content:
'Banana republic again': Former Costa Rican president slams Albanese ban
Former Costa Rican president and Nobel Peace Prize Laureate Oscar Arias Sanchez has criticised the government for denying entry to Francesca Albanese, the United Nations special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory.
“Today, we have once again been turned into a banana republic,” Sánchez said, according to journalist Paolo Mossetti.
El Premio Nobel de la Paz 1987, Ex Presidente de Costa Rica Oscar Arias, en viaje a Italia a reunión de Premios Nóbeles, fue a solidarizar con @FranceskAlbs en el aeropuerto en San José de Costa Rica https://t.co/KbSy0uTinR
— Paulina Astroza S. (@PaulinaAstrozaS)
November 28, 2026
Albanese, an Italian national, had travelled to Costa Rica to receive an honorary doctorate from the state-run University of Costa Rica. She was stopped at Juan Santamaria airport, which serves the capital, San Jose.
The Costa Rican government asserted that Albanese was the subject of an "international alert over links to terrorist acts".
Footage shared by Mossetti on X shows Albanese receiving a standing ovation at the university, with the rector apologising to her for her being stopped at the airport.
A standing ovation for Francesca Albanese at the University of Costa Rica, with the rector apologizing to her for her being stopped at the airport. “Today, we have once again been turned into a banana republic,” said Former Costa Rican president Óscar Arias Sánchez. https://t.co/YWKhRhlVJo

items.content:
Exclusive:
Uploading of intimate psychiatric information to wider medical records prompts some to shun support altogether
Some psychiatric patients are refusing treatment over the NHS adding intimate details from therapy sessions to their medical notes, fuelling fears that breaching privacy is posing a risk to health, the Guardian can reveal.
One stopped medical care for a heart condition when he discovered that details of intrusive sexual thoughts he’d experienced as result of obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) had been shared with a cardiac nurse.

items.title: UKMTO says five percent of ships attacked since 17 Aug sunk or lost
items.content:
UKMTO says five percent of ships attacked since 17 Aug sunk or lost
About 5 percent of vessels reported attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz have been confirmed lost or sunk since the Iran-US Memorandum of Understanding expired on 17 August, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).
Roughly 43 percent of ships in these incidents appear on the non-compliance list of the Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA), which was set up by Iran in May, UKMTO said in its weekly overview.
The PGSA blacklists ships it accuses of breaking its Hormuz transit rules, threatening fines, detention or confiscation. Its list passed 120 vessels in October.
According to the weekly overview, three tankers were struck by unknown projectiles within about 17 minutes on 22 November while heading east through the Strait of Hormuz. All three continued their voyages.
UKMTO documented 10 incidents in the week to 25 November, seven of them in the Strait of Hormuz.
Combined transits remain roughly 65 percent below pre-conflict levels, with 166 outbound and 173 inbound crossings last week. About 70 percent were energy carriers, and more vessels are using the southern route.

items.title: Iran's navy commander says country's maritime ports 'fully operational'
items.content:
Iran's navy commander says country's maritime ports 'fully operational'
Iran’s Navy commander, Rear Admiral Shahram Irani, has said the country's maritime ports were fully operational despite the "enemy's attempts to disrupt the economy", Mehr news agency reported, citing the state broadcaster, Irib.
Irani said the United States was forced to retreat to the Arabian Sea and northern Indian Ocean and warned that any further military operations "will push American forces out of the region and back to US shores".
He stated that a naval blockade is traditionally imposed before a war to pressure an adversary, but announcing one during an ongoing war amounts to an admission "that the enemy has failed" to achieve its military objectives, the report said.
“The enemy has not reached any of its malicious goals,” he said, warning that there would be "no geographical limits in confronting the enemy".
He said Iran would launch not just one, but a series of operations in case of "any mistake".

items.content:
Mohammad Baraka unable to access redundancy pay for almost 20 years’ service as family’s situation becomes ‘increasingly desperate’
A Palestinian man who worked for the EU in Gaza has told of a “devastating” struggle to survive after he was made redundant by bosses in Brussels.
He was let go last year after being evacuated to Egypt but his redundancy payment was made to an account to which he has no access. “My family’s situation has become increasingly desperate,” said Mohammad Baraka, a former staffer at the EU border assistance mission (EUBam).

items.title: Stunted sprouts: heatwaves and drought take toll on festive vegetable
items.content:
The Christmas staple is smaller this year after a hot, dry summer hit the water-loving – but versatile – brassica
They are a key ingredient in many Christmas dinners, but brussels sprouts appearing on diners’ plates this festive season are likely to be smaller than usual, after the hot, dry summer took its toll on the water-loving crop.
Sprouts are generally planted outdoors between March and early June, meaning they were already in the ground when the UK faced a series of heatwaves and
drought conditions
across Wales and most of England.

items.title: US activist returning from West Bank tour detained by Israeli police, UCPiP says
items.content:
US activist returning from West Bank tour detained by Israeli police, UCPiP says
Israeli police have detained Mel Duncan, co-founder of Unarmed Civilian Protection in Palestine (UCPiP), as he was returning to Tel Aviv after a tour of the occupied West Bank, the organisation said in a statement on X.
A US citizen from St. Paul, Minnesota, and a longtime advocate for nonviolence and civilian protection, Mel was not engaged in any illegal activity, UCPiP said.
"He was travelling on a bus full of Israeli citizens returning from a tour of the West Bank and heading towards Tel Aviv when Israeli police stopped the bus, held it for approximately an hour, and confiscated his passport. Mel was the only passenger detained," the statement read.
He is currently being held at Ma’ale Adumim police station, and the grounds for his detention remain unclear, the statement added.
His lawyer has requested urgent diplomatic intervention to ensure he is questioned tonight rather than spending two nights in detention. The organisation also urged the US Embassy in Israel, elected representatives and the international community to intervene and secure Mel's release.
🚨 URGENT ACTION ALERT: UCPiP Co-Founder Mel Duncan Detained by Israeli Police 27 November 2026 Mel Duncan, co-founder of Unarmed Civilian Protection in Palestine (UCPiP), a U.S. citizen from St. Paul, Minnesota, and a longtime advocate for nonviolence and civilian protection, was detained today by Israeli police. Mel was not engaged in any illegal activity. He was travelling on a bus full of Israeli citizens returning from a tour of the West Bank and heading towards Tel Aviv when Israeli police stopped the bus, held it for approximately an hour, and confiscated his passport. Mel was the only passenger detained. He is currently being held at Ma’ale Adumim police station. The grounds for his detention remain unclear. His lawyer has requested urgent diplomatic intervention to ensure he is questioned tonight rather than spending two nights in detention. We urgently call upon the U.S. Embassy, elected representatives and the international community to: ▪️ Intervene immediately to secure Mel’s release. ▪️ Ensure questioning takes place tonight without unnecessary delays. ▪️ Guarantee his safety, legal rights and access to consular assistance. Those who dedicate their lives to protecting civilians should not themselves become targets. Please circulate widely and contact the U.S. Embassy and your elected representatives immediately. Unarmed Civilian Protection in Palestine (UCPiP) https://t.co/kvfWQawXHk #FreeMelDuncan #ProtectTheProtectors #UCPiP

The United States Central Command (Centcom) has refuted the Iranian military's claim that Iran attacked the USS Abraham Lincoln on the first day of the war, or that the IRGC regained control of two Iranian oil tankers seized by the US forces.
In a post on X, Centcom also refuted Iran's charge that it was charging $2.5 million from ships to pass through the Strait of Hormuz.
An Iranian military commander made multiple FALSE claims concerning U.S. Forces over the past 24 hours: 🚫 CLAIM: The U.S. military stole two Iranian oil tankers and the IRGC’s navy retook the vessels while American troops on board slept. ✅ FACT: Iran no longer has a navy. The entire situation the Iranian military commander described is another fabricated lie. 🚫 CLAIM: Iranian naval forces struck aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN 72) on the first day of Operation Epic Fury, forcing U.S. forces to seek assistance from regional countries for evacuation support. ✅ FACT: The Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group was well defended and never struck by Iran as a result. In fact, the strike group completed a historically successful combat deployment to the Middle East and safely returned to the United States last month. 🚫 CLAIM: CENTCOM is charging $2.5 million to ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz. ✅ FACT: While U.S. forces and regional partners do control the Strait of Hormuz, there is no toll for passing ships. CENTCOM’s efforts have restored freedom of navigation through the international waterway. Thousands of ships and billions of crude oil barrels have transited the strait freely and safely under U.S. protection despite unwarranted Iranian aggression.
— U.S. Central Command (@CENTCOM)
November 28, 2026

items.title: Albanese says Costa Rican police refuse to release her despite court order
items.content:
Albanese says Costa Rican police refuse to release her despite court order
UN special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory, Francesca Albanese, says Costa Rican immigration police are refusing to release her from an airport despite a Constitutional Court order allowing her to go to a hotel.
“SHOCKING. The Constitutional Court of CR ordered that I am let out to go to a hotel and rest and the immigration police does not let me. Am I detained?? HELP,” Albanese said in a post on X.
In another post, she said that the staff of her carrier, Air France, were ignoring the court order to take her to a hotel.
"@airfrance staff are actively ignoring the ruling with excuses while I’ve been awake for 50hrs straight," she wrote.
Albanese, an Italian national, had travelled to Costa Rica to receive an honorary doctorate from the state-run University of Costa Rica. She was stopped at Juan Santamaria airport, which serves the capital, San Jose.
SHOCKING. The Constitutional Court of CR ordered that I am let out to go to a hotel and rest and the immigration police does not let me. Am I detained?? HELP.
— Francesca Albanese, UN Special Rapporteur oPt (@FranceskAlbs)
November 28, 2026

items.title: Israeli defence minister rejects army chief's call to detain violent settlers, report says
items.content:
Israeli defence minister rejects army chief's call to detain violent settlers, report says
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has rejected a new request from military chief of staff Eyal Zamir to authorise administrative detention orders against Israeli settlers involved in attacks against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, Kan reported.
Zamir told Katz at a security consultation on Thursday that further steps were needed amid rising settler violence, and called for administrative detention and restraining orders against perpetrators, the report said.
Administrative detention allows suspects to be held indefinitely without charge or trial. It is widely used against Palestinians, including children, but Katz halted its use against Jewish Israelis in November 2024. He has, in fact,  repeatedly boasted of doing so, while expanding its use against Palestinians.
Dozens of restraining orders, which bar individuals from parts of the West Bank, are awaiting Shin Bet approval, according to Kan. Channel 12 reported that 70 people suspected of involvement in such attacks were arrested in recent weeks, but Israeli courts released all of them without indictments.
Shin Bet chief David Zini, who belongs to the Orthodox nationalist Hardal camp, has consistently objected to movement bans. He has been accused of undermining the agency's unit tasked with tackling settler violence.
A surge in Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank this year has been condemned globally. (AFP)

items.title: Yemeni forces claim 121 Houthi fighters killed in 726 attacks
items.content:
Yemeni forces claim 121 Houthi fighters killed in 726 attacks
Colonel Majed al-Nuzaili, spokesman for Yemen’s government forces, claimed as many as 726 attacks had been carried against Houthi positions over the past 24 hours.
Al-Nuzaili said the operations, conducted as part of the “Dawn of Yemen” offensive, included 23 air strikes, 642 artillery attacks, 35 drone operations and 26 rocket strikes. They resulted in the killing or wounding 121 fighters and commanders, according to the state-run Saba news agency.
The attacks also destroyed or damaged 81 military vehicles and pieces of equipment, he added.

items.title: Denied entry, Francesca Albanese to leave Costa Rica after second night at airport
items.content:
Denied entry, Francesca Albanese to leave Costa Rica after second night at airport
Francesca Albanese, the UN special rapporteur on the Palestinian territories, who was denied entry into Costa Rica, says she would leave the country on Saturday after spending two nights at the airport.
“Second night in the airport. Guarded by security at every step. Unconfortable (sic) chairs. Noise. Bright light. Counting the hours till my flight tomorrow,” she wrote on X.
Second night in the airport. Guarded by security at every step. Unconfortable chairs. Noise. Bright light. Counting the hours till my flight tomorrow.
— Francesca Albanese, UN Special Rapporteur oPt (@FranceskAlbs)

items.title: Israeli military claims MSF workers killed in Gaza strike were Hamas members
items.content:
Israeli military claims MSF workers killed in Gaza strike were Hamas members
The Israeli military has said the two Doctors Without Borders (MSF) workers -- Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu Hasira and Ma’ad Yousef Ali Sabeh -- killed in an air strike on a clinic in Gaza City were members of Hamas.

items.title: Mecca Alliance meet stresses need for continuing joint efforts, Saudi minister says
items.content:
Mecca Alliance meet stresses need for continuing joint efforts, Saudi minister says
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have stressed the need for continuing joint efforts to support the "political and defence tracks" of the Mecca Defence Alliance, Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman said.
In a post on X, he said the second meeting of the Political and Defence Strategic Committee of the Mecca Defence Alliance "affirms our countries’ unified position and active role in addressing the current situation and the close cooperation and coordination it requires to strengthen security and stability".
On the sidelines of the meeting, Khalid bin Salman held talks with Turkey's Minister of National Defence, Yasar Guler.
"We commended the meeting’s outcomes and stressed the importance of continuing to strengthen and develop military and defence cooperation to serve our shared interests and achieve security and stability," he said.
The second meeting of the Political and Defense Strategic Committee of the Mecca Defense Alliance affirmed a 'unified position'. (Pic Saudi Defence Ministry)

items.title: IRGC says two oil tankers catch fire after hitting naval mines
items.content:
IRGC says two oil tankers catch fire after hitting naval mines
Two oil tankers have exploded and caught fire after striking mines near Oman's Khasab port and in the eastern part of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said.
In a statement carried by Iranian news agency, Irna, the IRGC Navy said one tanker struck a naval mine at the entrance to Khasab Port, while a second tanker travelling along an "unauthorised route" east of the Strait of Hormuz also exploded and caught fire.
"Like the tankers that exploded previously, these vessels were attempting to slip through the Strait of Hormuz undetected via a sham route by disabling their tracking systems. Both ultimately exploded and burned near the southern coastline and Khasab Port," the statement said.

items.title: Drone that killed two Italians in Kuwait was Iranian-made, says Italy's foreign minister
items.content:
Drone that killed two Italians in Kuwait was Iranian-made, says Italy's foreign minister
The drone used in the attack on
Kuwait
that killed two Italians was manufactured in
Iran
, Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said on Friday.
In an interview with the Italian press, Tajani said: "According to the investigations carried out by the Kuwaitis, the drone was manufactured in Iran."
The attack on Thursday also injured two other people.
It drew condemnation from many countries, and some, including
Syria
and
Saudi Arabia
, blamed Iran for it.
Meanwhile, Iran has denied launching the drone, with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi calling the incident "suspicious".
"The Iranians say it was not launched from Iranian territory, but, as you know, Iran's proxies, all of Iran's allies, have Iranian-made drones," Tajani told press.
"There will be investigations, and the Iranians have said they are ready to participate in a commission of inquiry alongside the Italians and Kuwaitis," he added.

The Iranians say it was not launched from Iranian territory, but, as you know, Iran’s proxies, all of Iran’s allies, have Iranian-made drones. There will be investigations, and the Iranians have said they are ready to participate in a commission of inquiry alongside the Italians and Kuwaitis. We will see.

items.title: Doctors Without Borders says two staff killed in Israeli 'direct hit' on Gaza clinic
items.content:
Doctors Without Borders says two staff killed in Israeli 'direct hit' on Gaza clinic
Two employees of Doctors Without Borders (MSF) were killed in an Israeli strike on one of the organisation's clinics in the Gaza Strip on Friday.
The strike was a "direct hit" on the clinic, the organisation said.
"We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, both watchmen, in an Israeli strike on one of our Gaza clinics tonight," MSF said in a post on X.
"Our premises were clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military," it added.
The organisation says these killings bring the number of MSF staff killed by Israel in Gaza to 17.
The attack on the MSF clinic, close to al-Shifa Hospital, brought the death toll from Israeli attacks across the strip on Friday to eight.
Earlier on Friday evening, another Palestinian was shot dead by Israeli forces in the al-Mawasi area, southwest of Rafah in the southern Gaza Strip, Wafa news agency reported.
🔴 BREAKING - We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, both watchmen, in an Israeli strike on one of our Gaza clinics tonight. This is a direct hit on MSF, bringing the total number of MSF colleagues killed in Gaza to 17. Our premises were clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military. We stand in solidarity with the families and loved ones of our colleagues. We call for accountability.
— MSF International (@MSF)
November 27, 2026

items.title: Several Palestinians beaten and detained in Israeli raids across occupied West Bank
items.content:
Several Palestinians beaten and detained in Israeli raids across occupied West Bank
Raids and attacks by Israeli forces and settlers across the occupied West Bank on Friday left at least three Palestinians injured and several detained.
Three Palestinians were injured and another, identified as Muhammad Daifallah Arara, was detained on Friday night after Israeli occupation forces raided his home north of occupied Jerusalem and assaulted those inside.
The three sustained injuries to their shoulders, limbs and abdomens after being beaten by Israeli soldiers, according to the Jerusalem Governorate.
Earlier, a group of Israeli settlers attacked the family's home, attempting to break down its entrance and storm its courtyard, before Israeli forces intervened and raided the house.
Israeli forces raided a residential cave in the village of Khirbet Khallat al-Daba'a in Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron, on Friday evening, assaulting its owner, detaining his family members and vandalising property inside, Wafa news agency reported.
The cave belongs to activist Jaber al-Dababseh, who was beaten by Israeli soldiers while his family members were detained.
On Friday evening, Israeli forces fired tear gas at Palestinian residents in the town of Beit Ummar, north of Hebron, during a raid. Israeli soldiers forced shop owners to close their stores.
In the village of Jayyus, east of Qalqilya, Israeli forces detained seven Palestinians after raiding their homes and ransacking their property.
Israeli settlers also continued their attacks across the occupied West Bank throughout the day. They attacked Palestinian vehicles in the Wadi al-Shaer area in the Salfit governorate, damaging at least two, locals told Wafa.
In the town of Za'tara, east of Bethlehem, settlers set up tents, raising fears among Palestinian residents that they could pave the way for a new Israeli outpost there.
Separately, a group of Israeli settlers dumped waste near a Palestinian home in the Turmus Ayya Plain, north of Ramallah.

items.title: Oman's stock market on track to beat all Gulf states in 2026
items.content:
Oman's stock market on track to beat all Gulf states in 2026
Submitted by
Sean Mathews
on
Fri, 11/27/2026 - 21:00
Oman's economy has emerged as a relative winner amid the Iran war thanks to its geography and diplomacy, experts say
A man views Rasool al-Adham Mosque from the corniche at Port Sultan Qaboos in Oman's capital, Muscat, on 5 February 2026 (Loic Venance/AFP)
Off
Oman’s
stock market is on track to be the best performer in the Gulf region in 2026, with its economic growth pulling ahead of neighbours, in a sign of how it is reaping gains from distancing itself from the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The MSX30 Index, which tracks the performance of Oman’s stock exchange, has soared 22 percent year-to-date.
Dubai's stock market, the Dubai Financial Market General Index, the region’s second-best performer, is up 8.7 percent year-to-date. Saudi Arabia’s Tadawul market is down 3 percent year-to-date.
For comparison, in the US, the SP500 index is up 6.4 percent year-to-date after a sharp selloff in AI and technology.
Both the Saudi and Dubai stock markets have clawed back the steep losses of earlier this year after the US and Israel launched a war on Iran.
But Oman's success is more interesting when one considers the anger US President Donald Trump directed at it during negotiations with Iran over the way to manage traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, which is comprised of Iran and Oman's territorial waters.
Trump threatened to “blow up” Oman, where his family real estate business has licensed its name for use on a golf resort.
Oman: From outlier to trailblazer
Tensions are still simmering between the US and Iran. The US has launched strikes on Iran and its vessels, while Iran has attacked ships in the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf countries.
Kuwait blamed Iran for a strike on Thursday that killed two Italian soldiers at a military site. Iran denied responsibility, but in recent weeks has launched strikes on Kuwait and Bahrain, both of which host US military bases.
'From outlier to trailblazer': How Oman offers a glimpse into the post-war Gulf
Read More »
Oman’s economic performance is due in part to its posture in the Iran war, experts say. Middle East Eye
reported in June
that Oman’s geography, diplomacy and business acumen would put it at the forefront of a new order emerging in the Gulf where Iran is emboldened and the US’s security umbrella clouded by distrust.
Muscat was a mediator between Tehran and Washington in the months before the war. Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr Albusaidi made a rare public plea for diplomacy just before the US-Israeli attack, which was ignored in Washington.
Despite lobbying against the war, in relative terms, Oman is attracting more interest from investors and companies as they look for a safe haven that has not come under intense Iranian attack.
Geography and US bases
Oman also sits outside the Strait of Hormuz and boasts a large Indian Ocean coastline.
Oman’s two main ports experienced an unprecedented surge in traffic during the war. Sohar port saw a 1,766 percent surge in ship destination change requests in March, while Salalah saw an 800 percent increase,
according
to maritime intelligence firm Windward.
'Vulnerability exposed': War on Iran will change how the US bases troops in Gulf
Read More »
Oman is also being eyed as a corridor to bigger neighbours like Saudi Arabia.
One of the most obvious reasons Oman has not borne the brunt of Iranian strikes is its decision not to join the US and Israel in attacking Tehran. It also has a different approach to basing the US military, which resembles that of some European countries.
Oman is the US’s oldest treaty partner in the Gulf, going back to 1833. But Oman hosts no permanent US military facilities or troops, unlike Bahrain, Qatar, Kuwait, the UAE and Saudi Arabia. Instead, the US has an “access agreement” to use Omani ports.
Albusaidi
said
earlier this year that the US was pursuing the war on Iran in the interest of Israel, and that Iran’s strikes on Gulf states hosting US military bases were ”inevitable”.
The International Monetary Fund estimates Iran’s economy to grow 4 percent this year, whereas every other Gulf economy is expected to contract, with the GCC overall shrinking 4.8 percent.

items.title: Israeli real estate company holds 'Black Friday' land sale in Brooklyn
items.content:
Israeli real estate company holds 'Black Friday' land sale in Brooklyn
An Israeli real estate group held a "Black Friday" event in Brooklyn on Wednesday, advertising property sales and promoting what activist group Pal-Awda termed "illegal settlement on stolen Palestinian land”.
Firecrackers, smoke bombs and eggs were thrown at protesters by pro-Israel demonstrators outside the real estate event.
Israel's
CapitIL
real estate agency held the event, selling property in Essen NY Deli in Brooklyn. CapitIL’s website advertises several properties in and around Jerusalem. None publicly advertised is in the occupied West Bank. Middle East Eye was not able to verify which part of Jerusalem the land being promoted was located in. East Jerusalem is occupied according to international law.
Pal-Awda, an organisation that advocates for Palestinian refugees' right of return to their homeland, organised the protest outside the real estate event.
A spokesperson for Pal-Awda called the event "discriminatory" and said they would protest the land sales “no matter where in Palestine the stolen land is located” and that “all of it was taken from dispossessed Palestinians, as part of the ongoing Zionist ethnic cleansing”.
The group says that these land sales violate several state and federal laws, including “New York Property Law, New York Human Rights Law, and state and federal real estate and housing laws”.

items.title: Eisenkot says Netanyahu dragging out coalition talks as deadline nears
items.content:
Eisenkot says Netanyahu dragging out coalition talks as deadline nears
Gadi Eisenkot, the Israeli opposition leader who is tasked with forming the next Israeli government, said on Friday that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been dragging out the negotiations, even though his Yashar Party is willing to agree on key points, Haaretz reported.
A former army chief of staff, Eisenkot has until 6 December to form a government, with the possibility of a 14-day extension, after October elections failed to give either camp an absolute majority.
According to Haaretz, sources close to Eisenkot's bloc expect Netanyahu to make a significant offer next week to prevent the government Eisenkot is planning from being sworn in.
Yashar and Likud met five times over the past two weeks to negotiate. Eisenkot said that Likud had refused on several days to schedule meetings as frequently as his party proposed.
"Two weeks and five meetings are a sufficient period in which an agreement could already have been reached, if they had wanted one," he said.

items.title: Israeli attacks across Gaza kill four Palestinians
items.content:
Israeli attacks across Gaza kill four Palestinians
Israeli attacks killed four Palestinians across the Gaza Strip on Friday, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
Several others, including a child, were wounded in a series of attacks across the strip.
In the southern city of Rafah, Gaza's civil defence crews recovered three bodies. They also rescued two wounded people after an Israeli strike near the Muawiya Mosque on al-Bahr Street, in the west of the city.
Wafa reported earlier on Friday that an Israeli drone struck a vehicle in the Bir al-Naaja area, west of the Jabalia refugee camp, killing a Palestinian man and wounding several others, some seriously.
Medical sources and eyewitnesses said Israeli forces stationed near the so-called "Yellow Line" repeatedly opened fire on tents sheltering displaced Palestinians in the area.
The so-called "Yellow Line" is a military boundary imposed by Israeli forces inside the Gaza Strip following the October 2025 ceasefire agreement.
Since the ceasefire came into effect in October 2025, more than 1,600 Palestinians have reportedly been killed and 5,833 injured.
Mourners carry the shrouded bodies of Palestinians killed in an Israeli air strike the night before, at Al-Shifa hospital in Gaza City, 26 November 2026 (Omar Al-Qattaa/AFP)

Israeli real estate company holds ‘Black Friday’ land sale in Brooklyn
Submitted by
Mounira Elsamra
on
Fri, 11/27/2026 - 16:33
Pro-Israel demonstrators threw fire crackers, smoke bombs and eggs at pro-Palestine protesters outside the event
Pro-Palestine protesters gather outside a "Black Friday" event an Israeli real estate company was hosting in Brooklyn, in New York City, promoting the sale of land in Jerusalem on 25 November 2026 (Mounira Elsamra/MEE)
Off
An Israeli real estate group held a "Black Friday" event in Brooklyn on Wednesday, advertising property sales and promoting what activist group Pal-Awda termed "illegal settlement on stolen Palestinian land”.
Firecrackers, smoke bombs and eggs were thrown at protesters by pro-Israel demonstrators outside the real estate event.
Israel's
CapitIL
real estate agency held the event, selling property in Essen NY Deli in Brooklyn. CapitIL’s website advertises several properties in and around Jerusalem. None publicly advertised is in the occupied West Bank. Middle East Eye was not able to verify which part of Jerusalem the land being promoted was located in. East Jerusalem is occupied according to international law.
Pal-Awda, an organisation that advocates for Palestinian refugees' right of return to their homeland, organised the protest outside the real estate event.
A spokesperson for Pal-Awda called the event "discriminatory" and said they would protest the land sales “no matter where in Palestine the stolen land is located” and that “all of it was taken from dispossessed Palestinians, as part of the ongoing Zionist ethnic cleansing”.
A spokesperson for the group said that these land sales are only open to vetted Jewish Americans who often have no previous or familial ties to Israel, arguing that CapitIL has ties to land sales happening in the occupied West Bank.
“Whether advertised or not, CapitIL and the event's other Israeli real estate cohosts like First Israel Mortgage have consistently offered or financed properties in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem during these events.”
The group says that these land sales violate several state and federal laws, including “New York Property Law, New York Human Rights Law, and state and federal real estate and housing laws”.
Chaos at the protests
Outside the event, it was chaos.
On Avenue J, 200 pro-Palestine protesters were kenneled in with lines of New York Police Department (NYPD) officers on either end and pro-Israel protesters sandwiching them in on both sides. NYPD drones loomed overhead, monitoring activity in the area. Newsweek reported that around 200 pro-Israel demonstrators were present, citing the NYPD.
Property sales of illegal Israeli settlement lands challenged in complaint in Canada
Read More »
Protesters chanted: “Palestine is our demand. No peace on stolen land.”
Pro-Israeli agitators threw at least three firecrackers and a red smoke bomb into the crowd of pro-Palestine protesters.
NYPD told MEE that three people had been arrested, processed and released, but did not specify which group they were from.
“We are being confronted by a racist mob of bigots who believe that Palestine does not belong to Palestinians, but belongs to settlers from all over the world. The people of Gaza are being bombed and murdered for the crime of being Palestinian in the land of Palestine, while these greedy companies are selling their Palestinian land to prosperous Americans who have no connection to Palestine whatsoever,” Pal-Awda activist Bill D told MEE.
MEE has reached out to CapitIL and NYPD for further comment but did not receive a response by the time of publication.
Protesters' Demands
Athena, a protester, was holding a sign depicting New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani pointing a gun with the words “Chief Executive of the SRG”, referring to the police department's Strategic Response Group.
Athena isn’t happy with Mamdani’s handling of Israel real estate land sale events in the city.
“We have a mayor who says that he's pro-Palestine and that he stands against the genocide. Yet he sends his police officers to defend Zionists selling stolen land in the United States,” she said.
Pal-Awda has four demands for the mayor. They are asking that he advance calls to the NY Attorney General Leticia James to investigate and audit "illegal Palestinian land sales" in the city; remove tax-exempt status from religious and educational institutions that host occupied West Bank land sale events; fire NY Police Commissioner Jessica Tish. They also want the mayor to “fully disband the Strategic Response Group (SRG) and its replacements that allow for the NYPD's ongoing brutalisation of our community”.
Mamdani announced the disbandment of the controversial SRG earlier this month, but officers in riot gear at the protest kenneling the demonstrators still wore shirts that said "Strategic Response Group".
The armour-clad SRG is made up of 500 highly trained NYPD officers who have become infamous for their “crowd control tactics” and mass arrests during protests in the city, where they use batons, tear gas, pepper spray and other “de-escalation” weapons on disruptive protesters.
The group came under particular scrutiny due to their crackdown on pro-Palestine protests at the height of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, particularly campus protests led by the student movement that started at Columbia University.
"The irony of the timing of Mamdani's announcement regarding the disbandment of the SRG is not lost on us tonight," a Pal-Awda representative said in a statement.
"We have no faith in the mayor's lofty words, when it is his NYPD that is trampling, strangling and brutalising those calling for the end of Zionist land theft in our city.
"Time and again, it becomes clear that all levels of city and state government - from Attorney General Letitia James, who allows illegal land sales to go unchecked, to Mayor Mamdani, who oversees the brutalisation of New Yorkers - remain deeply complicit in the sale of stolen Palestinian land."

items.content:
Former England Test cricketer was diagnosed with anxiety and depression before he took his own life in 2024
The wife of Graham Thorpe, the former England cricketer who took his own life, has started legal proceedings against an NHS trust after an inquest identified “failings” in his mental health care.
Thorpe died aged 55 in August 2024 in Surrey. His wife, Amanda, has lodged a personal injury claim at the high court against Surrey and Borders Partnership NHS foundation trust which was involved in his care, the Telegraph reported.

items.title: UN rights chief voices concern as Costa Rica bars Francesca Albanese
items.content:
UN rights chief voices concern as Costa Rica bars Francesca Albanese
Costa Rica denied entry to Francesca Albanese, the United Nations special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory, drawing
criticism
from UN human rights chief Volker Turk on Friday.
Turk said he was "deeply concerned" by Costa Rica's decision to bar Albanese from entering the country and urged authorities to reconsider after she was stopped at Juan Santamaria airport, which serves the capital San Jose.
Albanese, an Italian national, had travelled to Costa Rica to receive an honorary doctorate from the state-run University of Costa Rica.
The UN human rights office said on X that Albanese was denied entry on "claimed national security grounds".
The government of Costa Rica asserted that Albanese was the subject of an "international alert over links to terrorist acts".
An Italian lawyer, Albanese is the UN special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Palestinian territory, which has been occupied by Israel since 1967. She has been sanctioned by the United States since 2025.
"I am deeply indignant that the government of Costa Rica has spread false information that links me to terrorism," Albanese said from the airport, adding that she hoped Costa Rica would reverse the decision.
Israel's UN ambassador, Danny Danon, praised Costa Rica's decision in a post on X.
Under President Laura Fernandez, Costa Rica has deepened cooperation with the United States on security and moved closer to Israel. It signed a free trade agreement with Israel last year.

items.title: Canada's Supreme Court upholds law banning hijabs in Quebec public sector
items.content:
Canada's Supreme Court upholds law banning hijabs in Quebec public sector
Submitted by
Yasmine El-Sabawi
on
Fri, 11/27/2026 - 16:11
The country's former and only Islamophobia envoy calls the decision "devastating"
A view of the exterior of the Supreme Court of Canada in Ottawa, Ontario, on 12 July 2017 (Creative Commons)
Off
The Supreme Court of Canada on Friday
upheld
Quebec's highly contested 2019 law that bans religious symbols in the public sector.
It was, more than anything, seen to be targeting Muslim women in the province who wear the hijab, but also impacted Catholics, Sikhs and other minorities.
Quebec's population is
5 percent Muslim
, according to the last census carried out in 2021. That figure is second only to Ontario.
Amira Elghawaby, who was Canada’s first and only special representative on combatting Islamophobia, until her office
was shut down
earlier this year, called the verdict "devastating".
"The promise of Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms has been broken, and could be broken again and again. It means that religious freedoms, equality and the rights of all Canadians are no longer guaranteed," Elghawaby said in a statement released by the organisation she founded this year, the Muslim Communities Research Observatory.
“This ruling will instantly further impact the lives and livelihoods of Quebecers, particularly Muslim women who wear the hijab. In one study, 71% of Muslim women surveyed had considered leaving Quebec, with the province standing to lose an estimated $3.2 billion in income. It may also open the door for further violations of rights and freedoms," she added.
Technicality
Oftentimes rulings by the highest court come down to technicalities.
What the court was looking at in this case was the application of Section 33 of the constitution, known as the "notwithstanding clause", which shields Bill 21 from the Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
itself.
US midterm elections 2026: Record number of hijabis elected to statewide and national offices
Read More »
It was until recently rarely used, and even
seen as taboo
to invoke.
Former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said in 2022 that Canada's charter "cannot become a suggestion".
The Canadian Department of Justice
acknowledges
that it is a "unique" provision among constitutional democracies, because it allows the Canadian parliament or a provincial legislature "to derogate from certain sections of the Charter, namely section 2 (fundamental freedoms), sections 7 to 14 (legal rights) and section 15 (equality rights)".
Section 333 does not apply to voting, mobility or language rights.
"Once invoked, the notwithstanding clause prevents a court from declaring that legislation covered by a section 33 declaration is of no force or effect, despite any inconsistency in the legislation with the rights or freedoms under the listed Charter sections," the justice department says.
The notwithstanding clause is valid for a renewable five years.
"In short, Bill 21 is rooted in Quebec’s legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the laicity of the state in a free and democratic society," Supreme Court Chief Justice Richard Wagner said in Friday's ruling.
Impact
It was in 2019 that Quebec first passed the contentious law that bans public sector employees from wearing religious symbols - the Jewish kippah, Sikh turban or Muslim hijab, among others - on the job.
Bill 21 passed in a 73-35 vote at the time.
The rightwing Coalition Avenir Quebec government, which held a majority in the provincial legislature, invoked the notwithstanding clause to limit debate on the bill.
After it passed, Quebec's then-premier, Francois Legault, called it "a moment that Quebecers have long been waiting for".
"It's very clear, when we talk to Quebecers, that they want us to ban religious symbols for people in positions of authority," he added.
Within 24 hours, advocacy groups moved to challenge the law in court.
Among them were the National Council of Canadian Muslims and the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, who asked the Quebec Superior Court for an injunction to bar the province from implementing the law.
The groups said in a statement that Bill 21 "is unconstitutional and will cause irreparable harm to religious minorities" in the French-speaking province.
Quebec: Why are politicians attacking an effort to combat Islamophobia?
Read More »
Nearly two years later, in a
242-page ruling
, the Quebec Superior Court ruled that while Bill 21 has "serious and negative consequences for all those who wear religious symbols in public", it ultimately does not violate "the Canadian constitutional architecture".
Still, the court struck down parts of the bill, saying that English schools in the French-speaking province would be exempt from the ban.
It also said that members of the National Assembly, the provincial legislature, were
allowed
to wear religious symbols that covered their faces, such as the niqab.
Quebec has long had debates over the issue of secularism and the protection of minority rights.
In 2017, it passed
Bill 62
, which barred individuals from giving or receiving public services with their faces covered.
It was met with widespread public protests and was later suspended after a Muslim woman in Quebec who wears the niqab filed a legal challenge against the law, arguing it violated her constitutional rights.
Trudeau later called it "unthinkable" to "legitimise discrimination against citizens based on their religion".

items.title: Enemy should expect action in air and at sea, Iranian commander says
items.content:
Enemy should expect action in air and at sea, Iranian commander says
Iran's enemies should expect action in the air and at sea, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Aerospace Force commander Majid Mousavi said on Friday.
Breaking the blockade of Iran was the country's "firm mission and unwavering determination", he said in a post on X, referring to the blockade imposed by the United States on Iranian ports.
Speaking to the Iranian press on Friday, Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, said: "Neither will the Strait of Hormuz be opened, nor will we allow a blockade to remain in place."

items.title: The Com: the global cybercrime network posing a ‘chilling threat’ to children
items.content:
FBI estimates thousands of people identify as members, or recent members, of group linked to indecent images of girls and blackmail
It sounds benign: the Com, short for the Community. But crime agencies around the world warn that it is far from that and the young cybercriminals involved are causing havoc and putting children at chilling, sickening risk.
Beau-Jack Mensforth was jailed
by a UK judge on Friday for his activities as part of the Com. He was one individual operating from his bedroom in north-east England, but there are probably thousands more like him and parents are being urged by police to be aware and to check their children’s devices.

Dozens of Labour MPs in favour of Rosebank are putting pressure on the prime minister not to block the North Sea oilfield, warning that doing so could spell “lights out for Labour in Scotland”.
As many as 80 pro-drilling MPs are considering writing their own letter to Andy Burnham after
nearly 100 of their colleagues called on the prime minister not to allow the project to proceed
. Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra has also reiterated his support for Rosebank, cautioning that “working-class people in vocational jobs” were threatened by the decline of the North Sea basin.

items.title: Centcom says it disabled commercial ship trying to run Iran blockade
items.content:
Centcom says it disabled commercial ship trying to run Iran blockade
The US military said on Friday that it had disabled a commercial ship in the Gulf of Oman on Thursday after its crew attempted to run the US blockade of Iran.
Military aircraft launched precision munitions that struck the stern of the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer after it departed from the port city of Bandar Abbas.
It tried to transit regional waters, US Central Command (Centcom) said in a statement.
The ship's propulsion was disabled while the civilian crew was unharmed, it added.

items.title: Mecca pact members meet in Islamabad and condemn Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
items.content:
Mecca pact members meet in Islamabad and condemn Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
Ministers from
Turkey
,
Saudi Arabia
and
Pakistan
met in Islamabad on Friday to discuss their mutual defence agreement and reiterated their condemnation of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, Pakistan's foreign minister said.
The three countries pledged to intensify efforts to support the kingdom in "safeguarding its security, sovereignty and territorial integrity", Ishaq Dar said in a statement after the meeting.
They also reaffirmed their commitment to more cooperation in defence industries, training and capacity-building, the statement said.
The three countries signed a joint defence agreement in Mecca in August. Recently, countries such as
Syria
and Indonesia have also expressed interest in joining it.

items.title: US lobbied Iraq and Venezuela to exit Opec, sparking Saudi intervention
items.content:
US lobbied Iraq and Venezuela to exit Opec, sparking Saudi intervention
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Fri, 11/27/2026 - 15:57
The US pressed Iraq and Venezuela to leave the Saudi-led energy cartel over the summer in a bid to bring down prices
Representatives of Opec member countries attend a press conference after the 45th Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee and the 33rd Opec and non-Opec Ministerial Meeting in Vienna, Austria, on 5 October 2022 (AFP)
Off
The
US
tried to break the
Saudi Arabian
-led energy cartel Opec by lobbying
Iraq
and
Venezuela
to leave the organisation earlier this year, sparking a direct intervention from the Saudi Crown Prince, according to a report by Reuters.
The report, published on Friday, reveals how President Donald Trump’s bid to boost production and lower energy prices amid the war on Iran put the US in direct conflict with Saudi Arabia, one of the US's closest allies in the region, which also sells its oil in US dollars and hosts US troops.
The Trump administration’s lobbying over the summer also sheds new light on the decision of the
UAE to leave
Opec in May.
The Trump administration welcomed the move at the time. Washington extended the option of a
currency swap line
to the UAE to allow the Emirates to access US dollars if its reserves ran dry. The rare gesture came shortly after the height of fighting between the US and Iran, when oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz had plunged.
Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Venezuela, Iran and Kuwait were the founding members of Opec in 1960.
Iran is already outside the cartel’s purview as a result of US sanctions and its so-called “shadow sale” of oil to China. The withdrawal of Iraq and Venezuela from the alliance would have effectively spelled Opec’s demise, although the alliance has been under pressure for years.
Reuters reported that Iraq’s Prime Minister ‌Ali Faleh al-Zaidi, who was endorsed by Trump, raised withdrawing from the alliance over the summer in discussions with US officials, who encouraged the idea. Officials in Iraq’s oil ministry discouraged the idea, saying that Baghdad should push for a higher quota within Opec, allowing them to pump more oil.
Trump's Venezuela oil gambit depends on a 'swashbuckling' attitude the market lacks
Read More »
The discussions came amid Zaidi’s high-profile visit to Washington in July where he unveiled a raft of economic deals that he hoped would overshadow tensions with the US over Iran-aligned militias in Iraq.
Middle East Eye was the
first to reveal
that Iraq planned to resurrect a new oil pipeline through Syria to the Mediterranean with US backing.
The US has massive financial leverage over Baghdad because income generated from Iraq’s oil sales is deposited at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York instead of being sent to Iraqi banks.
The Trump administration halted dollar shipments to Iraq until Zaidi was named prime minister. He also received the backing of pro-Iran factions.
The US’s leverage over Venezuela is even larger since the Trump administration attacked the country and removed former President Nicholas Maduro from power at the start of the year.
The US effectively
seized control
over Venezuela’s finances and oil revenue, and tapped commodities trader Vitol to handle sales. Vitol is an
employee-owned
trading house headquartered in Switzerland.
Venezuela holds the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves, but the country has been unable to tap them due to a lack of investment.
Oil is classified by its density and sulfur content. The Venezuelan variety is heavy, which makes it expensive and labourious to extract, whereas Iraqi crude is light, making it cheap and easy to take out of the ground. Venezuela's oil needs to be refined, and while it has some domestic refineries, much of it is refined in the US, China and India.
Still, the US’s discussions with Venezuela so unnerved Saudi Arabia that the Crown Prince had to directly intervene to keep Venezuela paying its Opec dues.

items.title: Israeli drone strike on vehicle kills Palestinian man in northern Gaza
items.content:
Israeli drone strike on vehicle kills Palestinian man in northern Gaza
A Palestinian man was killed and several others were wounded on Friday evening in an Israeli drone strike on a vehicle in the northern Gaza Strip, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
The strike hit the vehicle in the Bir al-Naaja area, west of the Jabalia refugee camp, killing Khaled Assaf, witnesses told Wafa.
Some of the wounded were in serious condition.
Separately, a child was wounded by Israeli gunfire in Khan Younis, in the southern Gaza Strip.
Israeli forces stationed near the area's eastern perimeter repeatedly opened fire towards tents sheltering displaced Palestinians, wounding the child.
The Palestinian health ministry said on Thursday that Israeli attacks had killed at least 19 Palestinians and wounded 48 others over the past 48 hours.
The latest attacks brought the total number of Palestinians killed since the so-called ceasefire began in October last year to 1,705.

items.title: Gaza's children caught in the grip of a meningitis outbreak
items.content:
Gaza's children caught in the grip of a meningitis outbreak
For 10 days, two-month-old Mostafa Hallawin has been bedridden at Al-Rantisi Children’s Hospital in Gaza City. After suffering a persistent high fever, reaching 39C, and recurring abdominal swelling, the
Palestinian
infant was diagnosed with meningitis.
“It started with a skin rash and a high fever, with his temperature reaching 39C,” his mother, Amal, told Middle East Eye.
“Every day, doctors perform medical scans and laboratory tests,” she added, saying his condition has shown little improvement, largely because of shortages of essential medicines.
Hallawin is one of the most recent children to develop meningitis amid a spike in cases across the war-torn enclave, where
Israel
has all but destroyed the healthcare system and continues to ban essential medicines.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha)
reported
413 suspected meningitis cases in Gaza between 27 September and 31 October, including 294 viral and 119 bacterial cases. The report said 68 percent were recorded in Gaza City.
On Tuesday, the Palestinian Health Ministry declared an "epidemic alert" across Gaza, citing a sharp rise in meningitis cases and deaths.
Read more: Gaza's children caught in the grip of a meningitis outbreak
Nine-month-old Mohammed, who is being treated for meningitis, sits on his mother Reham Wahdan’s lap at Al-Rantisi Hospital in Gaza City (Hani Abu Rezeq/MEE)

items.title: Tunisia NGO slams 'inhumane' prison conditions after dozens of detainee deaths
items.content:
Tunisia's main rights group on Friday denounced "inhumane" conditions in Tunisian prisons, saying 30 inmates have died since the beginning of summer, the country's hottest on record.
Authorities have yet to release figures for prison deaths after a summer marked by multiple heatwaves, water shortages and power cuts.
"The situation in prisons is inhumane and catastrophic," said Bassem Trifi, head of the Tunisian League for Human Rights, adding that "overcrowding and the lack of healthcare" in prisons were a major issue.

items.title: Canada’s top court upholds Quebec law barring public sector workers from wearing religious symbols
items.content:
Closely watched decision exposes tensions between minority rights and the power of government to override those rights
Canada’s top court has largely upheld a
controversial secularism law
in the province of Quebec barring public sector workers from wearing conspicuous religious symbols, in a closely watched decision that exposes the tensions between minority rights and the power of government to override those rights.
In a 6-1 ruling
released on Friday morning
, the supreme court found Quebec was permitted to shield the law, Bill 21, from most court challenges on the grounds that it violated charter rights.
