items.title: Pro-Israel groups brand US Gaza advert 'antisemitic Hamas propaganda'
items.content:
Pro-Israel groups brand US Gaza advert 'antisemitic Hamas propaganda'
A 30-second advert highlighting
US
taxpayer funding for
Israel
was broadcast across the United States on Wednesday night during a Thanksgiving special edition of the long-running sketch show Saturday Night Live.
The ad, from the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project (Imeu), a pro-
Palestinian
advocacy group based in California, shows an American girl carrying out chores over the course of the year in order to make $400 to buy a new bicycle.
The footage then cuts from the American on a pristine suburban street to a Palestinian girl amid the rubble of Gaza. The Palestinian girl has lost a leg to Israeli bombs and is on crutches.
“Every three seconds, our government sends $400 of taxpayer money to Israel to do this,” says the ad's American narrator, against the backdrop of the girl in Gaza.
The US
currently officially gives
Israel $3.8bn a year, in a 10-year memorandum of understanding that runs from 2019 to 2028, working out at just over $360 every three seconds.
Read more: US broadcaster airs ad highlighting military aid to Israel during Saturday Night Live

items.title: What will change for Israel, Algeria and Morocco if Spain's right-wing wins elections
items.content:
What will change for Israel, Algeria and Morocco if Spain's right-wing wins elections
“The
Israeli
government has all our support, affection and understanding,” Santiago Abascal, leader of
Spain’s
far-right Vox party, said during a trip to Israel in December 2023.
While Abascal visited Israel in a show of support and to seek political backing from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Israeli forces had killed more than 16,248
Palestinians
in Gaza, according to figures cited by the UN humanitarian office, OCHA. About 70 percent were women and children.
Spain votes on Sunday, with polls predicting that Vox will almost double its parliamentary representation from 33 seats to 61.
That would help the centre-right People’s Party (PP), which polls project will win 129 seats, assemble a coalition comfortably above the 176-seat majority needed to unseat Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s centre-left government.
The election could also change Spain’s foreign policy, including its relationship with US President Donald Trump, its tense relations with
Morocco
and its deteriorating ties with Israel over
the genocide in Gaza
and ongoing apartheid policies in the occupied West Bank.

items.title: How Palestinian life in East Jerusalem is being extinguished
items.content:
How Palestinian life in East Jerusalem is being extinguished
"The first step in liquidating a people is to erase its memory. Destroy its books, its culture, its history. Then have somebody write new books, manufacture a new culture, invent a new history,” wrote the Czech novelist Milan Kundera.
“Before long that nation will begin to forget what it is and what it was. The world around it will forget even faster.”
Kundera’s subject was Czechoslovakia under Soviet communism. His words also apply to life as it is lived in East Jerusalem today under
Israeli
occupation. An extinguished city where people live abandoned lives of quiet desperation.
For
Palestinians
, any form of politics has become dangerous. All political activity - campaign meetings, press conferences, canvassing - is banned and punishable by jail.
The governor of Jerusalem appointed by the Palestinian Authority (PA), Adnan Ghaith, once a busy political activist in the Silwan neighbourhood southeast of the Old City, has been arrested 37 times in his seven years in office.
Evictions and erasure: How Palestinian life in East Jerusalem is being extinguished, by Peter Oborne in Jerusalem

items.title: UN refugee agency seeks $7.1 bn in 2027
items.content:
The United Nations' refugee agency said on Friday it was seeking a much-reduced $7.1 billion to protect stateless people and respond to emergencies in 2027.
UNHCR chief Barham Salih warned last month that his agency was being "asked to do the impossible", over-stretched by a huge funding shortfall and near record-high population displacements around the world.
UNHCR's 2026 appeal targeted $8.5 billion -- of which only $2.9 billion has been raised to date.

items.title: Spain elections: Israel’s ‘greatest’ far-right ally in Europe poised to shape next government’s foreign policy
items.content:
Spain elections: Israel’s ‘greatest’ far-right ally in Europe poised to shape next government’s foreign policy
Submitted by
Elis Gjevori
on
Fri, 11/27/2026 - 13:52
The Spanish right could enter government despite public hostility towards Israel, including among conservative voters
A campaign poster for Spain’s far-right Vox party leader Santiago Abascal ahead of this Sunday's general election (Reuters)
Off
“The
Israeli
government has all our support, affection and understanding,” Santiago Abascal, leader of
Spain’s
far-right Vox party, said during a trip to Israel in December 2023.
While Abascal visited Israel in a show of support and to seek political backing from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Israeli forces had killed more than 16,248
Palestinians
in Gaza, according to figures cited by the UN humanitarian office, OCHA. About 70 percent were women and children.
Spain votes on Sunday, with polls predicting that Vox will almost double its parliamentary representation from 33 seats to 61.
That would help the centre-right People’s Party (PP), which polls project will win 129 seats, assemble a coalition comfortably above the 176-seat majority needed to unseat Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s centre-left government.
The election could also change Spain’s foreign policy, including its relationship with US President Donald Trump, its tense relations with
Morocco
and its deteriorating ties with Israel over
the genocide in Gaza
and ongoing apartheid policies in the occupied West Bank.
Domestic issues, including the cost of living, affordable housing, wages and immigration, have dominated the campaign since Sanchez called the snap election on 5 October.
Those concerns have driven support for Vox and the PP more than any shift in public attitudes towards foreign policy.
According to a June survey by Pew Research Center, around 66 percent of Spaniards on the self-identified political right viewed Israel unfavourably, compared with 79 percent in the centre and 96 percent on the left.
“The historical and traditional stance held by all Spanish governments [towards Palestine] since the transition to democracy in the 1970s enjoyed a broad consensus across the political spectrum - among conservatives, socialists, left-wing parties, and nationalists alike - and commanded widespread public support,” said Isaiah Barrenada Bajo, an international relations professor at Complutense University of Madrid.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez speaks during a press conference after attending a special summit of European Union leaders in January (AFP)
Under former PP prime minister Jose Maria Aznar, who governed Spain from 1996 to 2004 and took the country into the
Iraq
war, “a shift occurred toward a neoconservative, more Atlanticist, and pro-Israel orientation,” Barrenada told Middle East Eye.
“This perspective has persisted within one faction of the PP to this day; it is especially prominent within the far-right party Vox - considered the most pro-Israel party in the European Parliament - upon which the PP might well depend to secure a governing majority,” he added.
Israel’s diaspora affairs minister, Amichai Chikli, called Abascal “a personal friend” and “one of Israel’s greatest supporters in Europe” during a podcast in April this year.
Abascal has also promised to reverse Spain’s recognition of a Palestinian state.
'One of the darkest episodes of this century'
Spain formally recognised the State of Palestine on 28 May 2024, alongside Ireland and Norway. Sanchez announced the decision in parliament six days earlier, summing up his reasons in three words: “Peace, justice and coherence.”
Sanchez has arguably been one of Europe’s strongest voices in demanding accountability for Israel’s crimes in Palestine.
Alongside recognising the genocide in Gaza, Sanchez said the bombing campaign against the besieged strip would become “one of the darkest episodes of this century”. He said he wanted Spaniards to be able to say they had stood “on the right side of history”.
Spain has also supported South Africa’s genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice.
“The recognition of the State of Palestine - though long overdue, having been demanded by parliament and civil society for over a decade - was welcomed by the majority of the population, regardless of whether they supported the current government or identified with the opposition,” Barrenada said.
'Historically, the Spanish right has been much firmer in responding to Morocco’s blackmail, hostility and pressure than the Socialist Party'
Taleb Alisalem, political analyst
Relations with Israel, meanwhile, have hit rock bottom since 2023. Both countries have withdrawn their ambassadors. Spain has sanctioned some Israeli settlers, banned imports from Israeli colonial outposts in the West Bank, introduced an arms embargo and condemned Trump’s plan to ethnically cleanse Gaza.
When more than 60,000
Moroccan
migrants crossed into the Spanish territory of Ceuta in August, many in Spain blamed Rabat and Tel Aviv for orchestrating the crisis. Israeli leaders relished the crisis, during which more than 100 Moroccans drowned attempting the dangerous crossing.
In September, Aznar, a staunch supporter of Israel, linked the Ceuta crisis to Spain’s deteriorating relationship with Israel. He
suggested
it resulted from "[alienating] the friendship of relevant allies, those allies one should be able to count on in crises". He called for the "normalisation of diplomatic relations with Israel as soon as possible".
The migration crisis emboldened the Spanish far right, which sought to portray Sanchez as weak on border security and unwilling to confront Morocco over its weaponisation of migrants.
“Historically, the Spanish right has been much firmer in responding to Morocco’s blackmail, hostility and pressure than the Socialist Party, which has consistently demonstrated an attitude of submission towards Rabat,” Taleb Alisalem, a Sahrawi writer and political analyst based in Madrid, told MEE.
“However, I personally do not believe that the People’s Party will go as far as reversing Pedro Sanchez’s decision to support Morocco’s autonomy plan for Western Sahara.”
Vox's unconditional support for Israel
Sanchez’s 2022 decision to back Morocco’s autonomy plan for Western Sahara proved controversial because it offers the territory limited self-rule under Moroccan sovereignty, while the Polisario Front seeks a referendum allowing the Sahrawi people to choose independence.
The move also triggered a rupture in relations with energy-rich
Algeria
.
“Could there be a rapprochement with Algeria? Certainly. Mainly because of energy interests. Algeria is a major gas producer with substantial reserves and supplies a significant proportion of the natural gas consumed in Spain. I believe a right-wing government would seek to rebuild and strengthen relations with Algiers,” Alisalem said.
Israel revels in Spain's migrant crisis while embarrassing ally Morocco
Read More »
“But Morocco also has considerable means of exerting pressure, extending far beyond its relationship with the Socialist Party. Rabat could also put pressure on the PP and even Vox, including through its close relationship with Israel.”
Latin America offers a recent precedent for how a change from a left-wing to a right-wing government can dramatically shift foreign policy towards Israel and the US.
In August, Colombia’s newly elected far-right government, led by Abelardo de la Espriella, recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara and Israeli sovereignty over the occupied Syrian Golan Heights. It also announced plans to move its embassy to west Jerusalem.
Moussa Bourekba, a research fellow at the Barcelona Centre for International Affairs and author of
Escalation within Continuity: Spain’s Foreign Policy towards Israel and Palestine after October 7th
, told MEE that Spain was unlikely to undergo such a dramatic shift.
During an election debate on Thursday, PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo described events in Gaza as “a massacre” and “unacceptable”.
“Vox clearly has a sense of unconditional support to Israel,” Bourekba said, adding that the “PP could not openly go against the move of recognition of Palestine, because that would mean going against what the Spaniards believe and think.
“My argument here is that the very same way that leftist parties within the current coalition government led by Sanchez have been very influential in pushing him to raise the tone against Israel, to adopt sanctions, and to show solidarity with Palestine, we could expect Vox to act in a similar manner with PP, but in the opposite direction.”

items.title: Newly released documents suggest CIA did more post-9/11 waterboarding than previously acknowledged
items.content:
Declassified documents appear to support belief that waterboarding was more common and may have occurred beyond two acknowledged sites
Newly released documents suggest that the CIA waterboarded more detainees during the post-9/11 “war on terror” than previously acknowledged, utilizing a site north of Kabul, Afghanistan, for the practice of simulated drowning.
The agency has acknowledged waterboarding three men: Abu Zubaydah, believed to be a high-ranking member of al-Qaida; Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, suspected architect of the 11 September 2001 attacks; and Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri, accused of planning the 2000 bombing of a navy destroyer.

items.title: Three studies link glyphosate to cancer, contradicting claims of Trump EPA
items.content:
Experts say NIH research raises concerns about chemical companies’ influence on US agency’s pesticide division
The US government’s top medical research agency has
released
three
new studies
linking glyphosate, the world’s most widely used pesticide and an active ingredient in Roundup,
to cancer
. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) findings contradicts a controversial recent Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) conclusion that the weed killer is not a carcinogen, and deals a blow to the White House, which has been
closely allied
with Roundup producer Bayer.
The NIH’s three papers could have significant political and legal fallout. The EPA is in the process of a court-ordered re-evaluation of glyphosate’s cancer risks. The NIH findings generates new pressure for the EPA to find that the substance is linked to cancer, which would subject it to a modest increase in regulations.

items.title: Evictions and erasure: How Palestinian life in East Jerusalem is being extinguished
items.content:
Evictions and erasure: How Palestinian life in East Jerusalem is being extinguished
Submitted by
Peter Oborne
on
Thu, 11/26/2026 - 15:39
Teachers arrested, bookshops shuttered, homes demolished, and violent settlers running amok – under occupation, no one is safe from brutal Israeli expansionism
"The first step in liquidating a people is to erase its memory. Destroy its books, its culture, its history. Then have somebody write new books, manufacture a new culture, invent a new history,” wrote the Czech novelist Milan Kundera.
“Before long that nation will begin to forget what it is and what it was. The world around it will forget even faster.”
Kundera’s subject was Czechoslovakia under Soviet communism. His words also apply to life as it is lived in East Jerusalem today under
Israeli
occupation. An extinguished city where people live abandoned lives of quiet desperation.
For
Palestinians
, any form of politics has become dangerous. All political activity - campaign meetings, press conferences, canvassing - is banned and punishable by jail.
The governor of Jerusalem appointed by the Palestinian Authority (PA), Adnan Ghaith, once a busy political activist in the Silwan neighbourhood southeast of the Old City, has been arrested 37 times in his seven years in office.
Symbols of national identity are not allowed. Fly a Palestinian flag and you will be arrested. The national anthem is banned. The authorities search schoolchildren's bags, then confiscate books carrying the PA logo. Shopkeepers in the old city are
banned
from selling T-shirts with Palestinian national symbols.
I asked a teacher what would happen if he flew the Palestinian flag. “They would close down the school,” he said.
What if he flew the Israeli flag? “They would send me flowers.”
He told me that a school celebration of the national poet Mahmoud Darwish was halted by the authorities.
“We are raising up a peace message in our schools,” he says. “Our only weapon is our books. Why are they treating our schools like this? We are preparing our students to go to university. Not to fight and not to kill.”
Israel replaces Damascus Gate name on East Jerusalem signs
Read More »
On Thursday, Israeli police
raided
and ordered the closure of Al-Shabat Comprehensive High School, an all girls school in the Wadi Al-Joz neighbourhood east of the Old City, on the grounds that they had found “incitement material”, including Palestinian Authority textbooks.
Israeli activists erase Arabic from street signs. Municipality workers are already taking down signs bearing the name Damascus Gate, in use since the early Ottoman period.
A meeting on Jerusalem’s Mamluk architectural heritage, especially splendid around western entrances to Al-Aqsa in the Old City, was stormed by police earlier this year and the organisers were arrested.
One Palestinian says: “We used to gather, but we are afraid of collaborators. Of private detectives. Of attack.”
Everyone remembers the
funeral
of Shireen Abu Akleh, the Al Jazeera journalist shot dead by an Israeli soldier while reporting from Jenin in the West Bank in May 2022, when Israeli forces attacked people with batons, causing mourners to drop the coffin on the ground.
So much for freedom of assembly. Freedom of speech is also suppressed. An East Jerusalem head teacher was held in detention during my stay in Jerusalem. She was not calling for violence or even resistance. She had publicly criticised the barbaric treatment endured by Palestinians in Israeli jails, described as “
torture camps
” by the Israeli human rights organisation B’Tselem.
Mob rule
Damascus Gate used to be a gathering place for Palestinians. Now it can turn into a place of terror.
Palestinians told me that gangs from Lehava, a far-right Jewish supremacist movement whose Hebrew name is an acronym for “Prevention of Assimilation in the Holy Land”, congregate there.
“They start hitting us,” I was told. “Throwing things at us. You cannot respond. If you do, you will be arrested on the spot. Most people go home before 7pm [5pm GMT], when it gets dark.”
In September, an elderly Palestinian, Ahmed al-Husseini, was chased and repeatedly beaten to the ground as he tried to pass through a crowd of men
described
in Israeli media as “an ultra-Orthodox mob”.
Film of this assault went viral. The person filming the incident was heard declaring in delight: “Wow, they’re fucking up an Arab.”
Israeli security forces standing nearby could be seen looking on without intervening.
Right-wing Jewish Israeli youths gather at Damascus Gate for the Jerusalem Day march through the Old City on 14 May 2026 (Reuters)
Almost all violence goes unreported. Young people are the most vulnerable. A teacher told me his students are regularly assaulted on the way to and from school, and nothing can be done to stop this.
A receptionist in an East Jerusalem hotel frequented by Israelis was attacked by settlers. When she complained, the manager told her to get used to it because it was part of the job.
This account is based on conversations conducted over a three-week period with Palestinians living in occupied East Jerusalem. Some of those interviewed gave permission to quote them by name, but most were reluctant.
I have chosen to leave all interviewees anonymous because it became clear in the course of my research that, for those I spoke to, East Jerusalem has acquired the characteristics of a police state.
Palestinians are subject to ubiquitous surveillance and constant monitoring. Israeli police monitor closed-circuit cameras and use tracking and monitoring tools to join WhatsApp groups and scrape social media content. They also run an extensive, well-developed network of secret informants.
The arbitrary power of the Israeli state has replaced or bypassed every legal or judicial safeguard.
Palestinians live in fear of being hauled into al-Moskobiyya. The notorious Israeli detention facility takes its Arabic name from the local district known as the Russian Compound, which sits just outside the New Gate linking the Old City’s Christian Quarter to West Jerusalem.
During the mandate period, the British held and tortured Jewish prisoners there. More recently, it has become the local headquarters for the Shin Bet, Israel’s security service.
Palestinians speak of abuse inside the jail, recounting stories of sexual humiliation for women and torture (frequently involving anal rape, with sticks) for men.
Accounts of cruelty and torture inflicted on Palestinian detainees in Israeli prisons are taken seriously and documented by Israeli, Palestinian and international human rights groups such as
B’Tselem
,
Addameer
and
Amnesty International
.
“I have never seen my people terrorised like today,” one Palestinian intellectual remarked to me.
He explained that there were, in his view, three reasons for Palestinian political numbness in East Jerusalem.
“First, we have been watching the genocide in Gaza. You can see how Palestinian life is worth nothing to Israel,” he said.
The second factor, he said, was the oppressive presence of the Israeli police. Palestinians suffer grave punishment even for writing a social media post.
“You can be prevented from working, arrested, and imprisoned. Bus drivers have lost their job because of a post years ago.”
'Prison is not the same'
The third factor, he continued, is torture: “If you go to prison today, it’s not the same as it was. Nobody gets out of today’s prisons physically and psychologically sound. The levels of torture are beyond all imagination. One month of prison today is worse than several years in prisons in the past.”
He described accounts he had heard of beatings, rape and deprivation, then added: “The International Red Cross is not allowed to visit and we have found that, when lawyers do get access, prisoners beg them not to visit again because after the visit the prison guards beat them up and torture them as punishment.
“So now the only news we get is from those who come out of prison. They come out brutalised. There have been cases where they come out with their anuses so damaged that the bleeding cannot be controlled.”
Israel has barred the International Committee of the Red Cross from visiting Palestinian detainees since October 2023. In September, a Red Cross team met Israeli officials at a military detention facility after Israel’s Supreme Court ruled that its access to detainees should be restored.
The Red Cross
called
the meeting “a step in the right direction”, but visits to detainees have not resumed.
Occupied by Israel since 1967, East Jerusalem had until quite recently nonetheless sustained a relatively rich civil society with its own history of activism and protest.
Consider the
protests
five years ago involving sit-ins, neighbourhood gatherings and the raising of Palestinian flags against the expulsion of Palestinians from the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood.
In 2017, Palestinians
protested
against Israeli plans to install metal detectors around the Al-Aqsa complex by boycotting the site and praying outside. Israeli security forces violently cracked down on the protesters, but the government was forced to withdraw the plans.
Palestinians pray outside Jerusalem's Old City in protest over new measures at the entrance of Al-Aqsa Mosque in July 2017 (Reuters)
That kind of civic resistance has been quashed. I learnt of one senior activist, well known and respected in his professional field, who had recently emerged from an Israeli jail. Because of his political activities, he had been inside prisons often, and had always emerged strong despite the suffering he had endured.
This time, according to a friend who knew him well, he came out broken. He has explained to colleagues that he will never return to political work. He could not endure the same torture again.
War on civil society
Israel is waging a merciless war on Palestinian civil society.
In 2021, several leading Palestinian civil society and human rights groups were proscribed by Israel as terrorist organisations. They included the prisoner support organisation Addameer; human rights group Al-Haq; the Union of Palestinian Women’s Committees; and the Ramallah-based Bisan Center for Research and Development, which helps women who have been victims of violence.
Any organisation is now vulnerable. Earlier this month, the Abnaa al-Quds (Sons of Jerusalem) sports club in the historic al-Sadiya neighbourhood in the Muslim Quarter of the Old City was
closed
under an order issued by Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir.
Israel raids beloved Palestinian bookstores and detains owners
Read More »
The Israeli authorities raided and closed Maktabat al-Quds (Jerusalem Library), a cherished Arabic bookshop, in February 2025. The Educational Bookshop, a 40-year-old literary hub on  Salah al-Din Street just north of the Old City, has been
raided
twice, with the owners arrested and books seized.
In January, Israeli forces raided the Yabous Cultural Centre to stop screening of
Palestine 36
, the highly acclaimed Oscar-nominated film which tells the story of the 1936-39 Palestinian revolt during the British Mandate.
Three years ago, Palestinian schools in East Jerusalem went on strike in reaction to an attempt by the Jerusalem municipality to censor Palestinian textbooks and introduce an Israeli curriculum in classrooms.
Christian and Muslim worship is under attack. I was in the Old City at one of the entrances to Al-Aqsa Mosque with a Palestinian friend as settlers streamed past us during one of their regular invasions of the site. One settler suddenly halted, turned towards us, and addressed my friend in Hebrew.
My friend told him that he did not understand, but the settler talked back regardless, becoming angry and aggressive. Eventually, he left us alone and continued his journey up the steps into the compound.
My companion, who understands Hebrew well, explained the settler had been repeating aggressively: “Do you know what I am going to do tonight? I am going to Al-Aqsa Mosque where I will drink wine. What do you think about that?”
As the settler would have known, this was a grossly offensive and insulting suggestion. My friend pretended not to speak Hebrew to avoid a confrontation. If he had shown anger, he probably would have been arrested.
“In the past you could be rude,” a Jerusalem lawyer explains. “Now you cannot respond. The police are totally on the side of the settlers, to protect them when they provoke a fight.”
The settler was taking advantage of this impunity for Israeli Jews to insult a Palestinian’s religion.
Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir displays an Israeli flag inside Al-Aqsa Mosque complex during a settler raid in May 2026 (X)
Inside Al-Aqsa, Israeli security forces are ubiquitous, with an Israeli police station set up at the centre of the compound. Mosque workers cannot repaint their offices or mend a water pipe without Israeli permission. This year, even picking olives from the trees within the compound - a tradition stretching back to time immemorial - has been
criminalised
.
The walls of the ancient prayer hall at the southern end of the site are pitted with bullet holes, where Israeli forces have
opened fire
on worshippers. This defies international law, as well as the Ottoman-era Status Quo agreement that has governed interfaith relations in the Old City for hundreds of years.
Not even the dead rest in peace. It is heartbreaking to visit the 1,400-year-old Bab al-Rahmah Cemetery just outside the outside wall of Al-Aqsa, where Israeli security forces routinely damage gravestones and knock down tombs.
The Mamilla Cemetery in West Jerusalem dates back to the time of Sultan Saladin. Israel has destroyed hundreds of ancient graves here, digging up human remains to clear ground for development projects. Part of the site is now occupied by the Simon Wiesenthal Center's
Museum of Tolerance
.
'Urban renewal' and ethnic cleansing
The term East Jerusalem came into common use when the city was physically divided after the 1948 Arab-Israeli war. East Jerusalem, which includes the Old City, became part of Jordan. The west of the city came under Israeli rule. This arrangement persisted until 1967, when Israel annexed the Old City and East Jerusalem.
This move breached the Geneva Conventions. Even the United States, Israel’s great ally, voted for UN Resolution 242 in 1967, calling on Israel to withdraw from the occupied territories.
But the Knesset, Israel’s parliament, greatly expanded Jerusalem’s municipal boundaries, gerrymandering the area to exclude Arabs and create space for Israeli settlements.
This programme continued with demolitions of Palestinian houses enabled by a Janus-faced legal system that supported Israeli demands while ignoring Palestinian rights. There was, however, no wholesale act of ethnic cleansing - with one exception.
On 10 June 1967, 619 inhabitants of the Mughrabi Quarter were given three hours to evacuate. Immediately, bulldozers moved in to demolish this exquisite part of the Old City, founded in the 12th century by al-Malik al-Afdal, a son of Saladin, to provide accommodation for Muslim scholars and pilgrims from North Africa.
Teddy Kollek, then mayor of Jerusalem, mandated this destruction to create space for Jewish pilgrims who wished to visit the Western Wall.
The scholar
Karen Armstrong
wrote in 1998: “This was only the first act in a long and continuing process of ‘urban renewal’, a renewal based on the dismantling of historic Arab Jerusalem and in which demolition, archaeology, and a selective preservation of antiquities all play their part in imposing a new Jewish identity on the city.”
Now, Israel has returned to a programme of destruction that is far more wide-ranging and audacious than that undertaken by Kollek six decades ago.
Israel is evicting Palestinians through a massive programme of home demolitions while installing new settlements that will isolate East Jerusalem by cutting it off from the West Bank.
The attack on foreign consulates and NGOs is part of the programme to cut East Jerusalem Palestinians off from the world. Earlier this year, Israeli demolition crews with bulldozers moved in to destroy the UN Palestinian refugee agency (Unrwa) offices in Sheikh Jarrah. The expulsion of British diplomats and downgrading of the nearby British consulate was part of the same project.
Employees of the Israeli authorities remove belongings from a Palestinian home in the Silwan neighbourhood of East Jerusalem on 25 March (Faiz Abu Armila/MEE)
One of Israel’s weapons is biblical heritage. I accompanied a group of diplomats to al-Bustan (The Orchard), a neighbourhood a few hundred metres south of the Old City at the southern tip of the Mount of Olives.
It is destined to make way for a recreation area and car parks, with the entire neighbourhood renamed the "King’s Garden" despite doubt among scholars about whether any connection truly exists between al-Bustan and the royal gardens of ancient Israelite kings.
Half of the area’s 1,500 Palestinians residents have already been forced out, with the rest scheduled to be made homeless within a year.
Packed suitcases
Many houses have already been demolished. We met a grandfather standing in front of the ruins of what used to be his family home. He lives in a caravan outside, but a demolition order has been served on that, too.
Two packed suitcases stand by the front door. He explains that bulldozers can come without warning at any moment, leaving no time to pack. I ask him where he and his wife will live.
“We don’t know. Some people are now sleeping in cars.”
Another East Jerusalem neighbourhood is demolished as the world fails to act
Read More »
He takes us around his neighbourhood. On the right is a playground, also marked for destruction. On the left is a condemned football pitch.
Everything will be destroyed. Property. Public amenities. Communities. Families. Lives.
The grandfather makes a despairing plea to the diplomats: “We ask the world to pressure Israel not to demolish our remaining homes. The international community is allowing Israel to be above international law. “
We climb some steps into the living room of another house. It belongs to a blind man in his 50s who is challenging his demolition order in court.
“I am disabled,” he says. “I live with my wife, who is also disabled, and our son, whose house has already been demolished. In my situation, how do I look for a home? Even if there was a place to go, how could I afford the 6-7,000 shekels a month?”
Our expert guide Danny Seidemann, a Jewish Israeli lawyer, told us of other neighbourhoods scheduled for demolition, describing a “government programme” to encircle the Old City.
“The primary objective is a radical transformation of Jerusalem, establishing the presence of a specifically Jewish biblical messianic narrative which is being etched into the landscape of the settlement project, fragmenting Palestinian East Jerusalem and marginalising the Christian presence,” he said.
“They are establishing a Jerusalem where one empowered stakeholder is Israel - and a specific interpretation of Israel - and all others are minorities who live here at our pleasure.”
Nothing and nobody is safe. Last June, the Jerusalem municipality seized land in al-Bustan, south of the Old City, belonging to the Monastery of St Onuphrius. The Greek Orthodox Patriarchate ineffectively protested what it called  “an unlawful and illegitimate seizure of established Church property in the heart of Jerusalem”.
Earlier this month, resident Mahdi Tounsi, a student at Hebrew University, was seized from his dorm by Israeli police.
When he appeared by video link at a court hearing last week, there was visible bruising on his face. According to Israeli media, Tounsi has told his lawyer that police beat him in the dorm, later in their patrol car and also at the police station.
'Collective deterrence': Detention of Palestinian student in Israel fuels fears of wider crackdown
Read More »
Interrogators reportedly questioned him about his activism with Israeli-Palestinian organisations Standing Together and Ir Amim.
Standing Together is the largest Arab-Jewish grassroots organisation in Israel. It opposes the occupation of Palestinian territories.
Ir Amim is an Israeli non-profit which monitors events in East Jerusalem where it works to ensure the "dignity and welfare of all its residents and that safeguards their holy places, as well as their historical and cultural heritages".
Both groups have called for Tounsi's immediate release, while warning against using security agencies to silence political activity.
As this article went to press, Tounsi is still held under administrative detention, which allows suspects to be held for long periods without charge. According to Human Rights Watch, more than 3,000 Palestinians are currently in administrative detention.
After our tour, I walk away up the hill. In these streets Israeli settlers, some armed with assault rifles, have become a familiar sight. This is now legal under Israeli law. In March, Ben Gvir - himself a settler -
announced
that all Israeli Jewish residents of Jerusalem, including East Jerusalem, would be allowed to carry firearms.
As I prepare to leave East Jerusalem, I attend a play at the Palestinian National Theatre (el-Hakawati) in Sheikh Jarrah. The building, once a cinema, as the
Jerusalem Story
puts it, has an “unfortunate history”. It was, according to the website, “hit by an air missile in the June 1967 war and later torched by religious fundamentalists who believed that it showed erotic films”.
Actors set to work restoring the burnt-out shell and reopened it as a theatre in May 1984, and it has since provided space for artists to stage plays, mime performances, carnivals, workshops and seminars.
It has faced problems, including repeated threats, bans and temporary closures. Last November Israeli security forces stormed the building just minutes before a children's musical,
Dreams Under the Olive Trees
, was about to start. The audience was given five minutes to empty the theatre. Children were in tears and inconsolable.
The closure of the occupied West Bank and Gaza, the permit regime and the separation wall now make it all but impossible for Palestinians from beyond East Jerusalem to attend the theatre’s productions.
In an effort to overcome this, the theatre developed a mobile theatre and works with artistic and cultural institutions around Palestine to share its cultural output as widely as it can.
A scene from El Manshiyyeh, performed at the Palestinian National Theatre (Facebook)
Tonight’s play,
El Manshiyyeh
, scripted by the playwright Samer al-Saber, tells the story of two families in the eponymous neighbourhood of Jaffa before the outbreak of the Second World War.
It begins as a lively but generally carefree comedy about family disputes, business problems, and love affairs, set against the backdrop of British occupation.
In the second act, the British depart and Jewish militias arrive. The cheerful protagonists of the play’s first act face terrible decisions about whether to leave or to stay, and what to do with possessions.
As the fighting worsens, they have no choice but to flee. Amid the chaos, they get separated. Some take the boat to Beirut, others to Egypt, others head to Gaza.
By this point, the play is almost too painful to watch. I look around at the audience of about 300, mainly young Palestinians. Will history repeat itself as they too are evicted and made refugees? Are they watching their own future? Will they face the fate of
El Manshiyyeh families
as chronicled in Saber’s play?
That is the direction of travel in East Jerusalem. It is hard to see what will stop it. As this article was being prepared for publication, Israeli police
stormed
the Palestinian National Theatre once more during a musical event and kicked out the audience.

items.title: War, fear drive Sudanese writer Baraka Sakin's fiction
items.content:
A lifetime of war and persecution has shaped the writing of Sudanese novelist Abdelaziz Baraka Sakin, who has turned the fear and longing that are so central to his experience into his main drive.
The 63-year-old fled Sudan for Europe in 2012 and then returned, dreaming of an end to his forced exile.
But the war that erupted in 2023 and killed more than 200,000 people pushed him out again.
Still, he keeps writing.

items.title: UK government deleted record of meeting between Blair and Shabana Mahmood
items.content:
UK government deleted record of meeting between Blair and Shabana Mahmood
The British government deleted the record of a meeting between former prime minister Tony Blair and Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood,
according to the Democracy for Sale newsletter
.
The meeting, which took place in June 2025 when Mahmood was justice secretary, was originally declared as official government business, with its purpose listed as "stakeholder engagement".
But when we asked for details of what was discussed under the Freedom of Information Act, the Ministry of Justice told Democracy for Sale it was a "party-political" meeting and that no records of it existed.
Several days after the newsletter asked the government for comment, the meeting disappeared from the public register.
Blair is a member of US President Donald Trump's Gaza "Board of Peace", while Mahmood has pushed for increasingly draconian legislation on migration and maintained the government's ban on Palestine Action.

items.title: Turkey asks Georgia to investigate police violence against Besiktas fans in Batumi
items.content:
Turkey asks Georgia to investigate police violence against Besiktas fans in Batumi
Submitted by
Ragip Soylu
on
Fri, 11/27/2026 - 11:08
Ankara also summons the Georgian ambassador for a dressing-down as all 16 fans are released from police custody
Police use pepper spray on Besiktas fans after they unfurled a pro-Palestinian banner during their Europa League match against Hapoel Be’er-Sheva on Thursday night (Besiktas FC/Screengrab)
Off
Turkey
has asked Georgia to launch an inquiry into police violence against Turkish fans during Besiktas’s match against
Israeli
club Hapoel Be’er-Sheva in Batumi on Thursday night, diplomatic sources told Middle East Eye.
The sources said the Turkish government had demanded action against those responsible. Georgian police moved against Besiktas fans who unfurled a pro-Palestinian banner during the Europa League match.
Turkish officials also summoned the Georgian ambassador to the foreign ministry over the crackdown. The ministry was expected to reprimand the ambassador over footage showing police attacking the fans.
Local police arrested 16 Besiktas fans. Footage of the police intervention sparked public outrage in Turkey and drew condemnation from ministers and opposition leaders.
“The Turkish ambassador in Tbilisi also conveyed our strong protest regarding the police intervention,” a Turkish diplomatic source said.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan called his Georgian counterpart, Maka Botchorishvili, on Thursday night, the source said.
“Officials from the Turkish embassy in Tbilisi and the consulate general in Batumi are at the stadium. All necessary steps are being taken to ensure the safety of our citizens and protect their rights,” the source added.
Besiktas said they had filed an official complaint with European football's governing body Uefa over "disproportionate" use of force by the police.
Uefa moved the game from Istanbul to Batumi for safety reasons, but it had to be suspended in the 25th minute after police moved to take the banner down, leading to clashes between Besiktas supporters and police. The match was resumed after a 30-minute break.
Turkish Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci and Justice Minister Akin Gurlek also spoke with their Georgian counterparts and secured the release of the 16 fans, Turkish officials said.
Filistin’e özgürlük! 🇵🇸
Gürcistan’da Filistin halkıyla dayanışma amacıyla Filistin bayrağı açan Beşiktaş taraftarlarına yönelik güvenlik güçlerinin orantısız müdahalesini kınıyor; yaralanan taraftarlarımıza acil şifalar diliyoruz.
Mazlumların sesi olan Beşiktaş camiasının ve…
pic.twitter.com/mmfu9ViX84
— YENİ Parti iletişim (@yeniiletisiim)
November 26, 2026
“The intervention against our fans who unfurled a Palestinian flag and called for ‘Freedom for Palestine’ at Besiktas’s match against an Israeli team in Georgia is unacceptable,”
said
Numan Kurtulmus, speaker of the Turkish parliament.
“Supporting the brotherly Palestinian people’s struggle for freedom as part of the ‘Humanity Front’ rising around the world is a matter of conscience and moral responsibility. Responding with violence to this dignified stance is incompatible with the universal values of sport and constitutes a clear violation of fundamental rights and freedoms.”
Several ministers, including Turkish Sports Minister Osman Askin Bak, also criticised the police intervention.
Turkey’s main opposition party, Yeni, or “New”, issued a statement: “Freedom for Palestine! We will continue to stand in solidarity with the Palestinian people’s struggle for freedom, justice and peace.”
Musavat Dervisoglu, the leader of IYI, another opposition party, also condemned the intervention. He noted that Besiktas had been forced to play their home match abroad for security reasons, yet their fans had still faced violence.
Turkey and Georgia enjoy stable relations and cooperate in several areas, including energy and transport. Diplomatic crises between the two countries are rare.

items.title: US broadcaster airs ad highlighting military aid to Israel during Saturday Night Live
items.content:
US broadcaster airs ad highlighting military aid to Israel during Saturday Night Live
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Fri, 11/27/2026 - 11:20
'Every three seconds, our government sends $400 of taxpayer money to Israel to do this,' says advert, over backdrop of amputee child in Gaza
A screengrab from the advert (No More For Israel)
Off
A 30-second advert highlighting
US
taxpayer funding for
Israel
was broadcast across the United States on Wednesday night during a Thanksgiving special edition of the long-running sketch show Saturday Night Live.
The ad, from the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project (Imeu), a pro-
Palestinian
advocacy group based in California, shows an American girl carrying out chores over the course of the year in order to make $400 to buy a new bicycle.
The footage then cuts from the American on a pristine suburban street to a Palestinian girl amid the rubble of Gaza. The Palestinian girl has lost a leg to Israeli bombs and is on crutches.
“Every three seconds, our government sends $400 of taxpayer money to Israel to do this,” says the ad's American narrator, against the backdrop of the girl in Gaza.
The US
currently officially gives
Israel $3.8bn a year, in a 10-year memorandum of understanding that runs from 2019 to 2028, working out at just over $360 every three seconds.
The package also includes $3.3bn in foreign military financing and $500m in cooperative missile defence programmes, meaning that the advert's figure is accurate.
An advert criticising US taxpayer funding for Israel has come under criticism from Israeli media, politicians and pro-Israel US figures.
The 30-second clip was aired by broadcaster NBC across the US on Wednesday during the Thanksgiving edition of the Saturday Night Live show.
pic.twitter.com/aRktY1wr4P
— Middle East Eye (@MiddleEastEye)
November 27, 2026
At the end of the ad, the viewer is directed to a website called
No More For Israel
, which tells you that "the US government has sent Israel over $330bn in inflation-adjusted dollars since 1948. That’s $400 every three seconds non-stop for nearly 80 years."
"Right now, behind closed doors, the White House is negotiating a new long-term weapons giveaway to Israel that is estimated to send at least $19bn more of our tax dollars to Israel over the next five years: another $400 every three seconds," the site says.
'Antisemitic Hamas propaganda'
Israeli newspapers, the country's foreign ministry and pro-Israel figures in the US have hit out at broadcaster NBC for airing the advert.
End Jew Hatred, a group
linked
to the Lawfare Project,
called
the advert "antisemitic Hamas propaganda" and circulated a petition demanding that NBC stop broadcasting it.
Sex, drugs, Israeli tech and Trump rivalries: Five explosive claims from Kushner-UAE book
Read More »
Jonathan Greenblatt, CEO of the Anti-Defamation League,
wrote on X
: "Broadcasting an ad that blatantly demonizes the Jewish state and makes false claims about the use of American taxpayer dollars during primetime on the eve of a family holiday isn’t just insensitive. It’s indefensible.
"Again and again, why do people in positions of authority fail to demonstrate basic decency, let alone respect, for the Jewish community? At a moment of escalating antisemitism, there is no rationale to justify fanning the flames with such a twisted narrative."
Greenblatt did not elaborate on what the "twisted narrative" of the advert was or offer any evidence for why its claims were "false".
Self-described "accidental activist" Samantha Ettus said that the advert "promotes the lie that Israel deliberately targets children", more than 22,000 of whom have been killed in Gaza by Israel. "It never mentions Hamas. It never mentions October 7, the hostages, or the rockets Israel is defending against,"
Ettus posted on X
.
Israel’s foreign ministry said: “Don’t let anyone exploit your loved ones’ compassion this holiday season. Ask who’s funding this campaign, whose real goal is the destruction of Israel.”
“We are airing this ad because the American people deserve to know where their money is going,” Margaret DeReus, Imeu's executive director,
told
Semafor.
Viewing figures for Wednesday's broadcast have yet to be released, but last year's Thanksgiving special attracted approximately 2.7 million viewers.

items.title: Was Andy Burnham right to accept his award from the Muslim-baiting Spectator?
items.content:
Was Andy Burnham right to accept his award from the Muslim-baiting Spectator?
Submitted by
Peter Oborne
on
Thu, 11/26/2026 - 15:53
These cross-bench jollification ceremonies might appear innocent at a glance - until you dig deeper into the magazine's coverage of Islam
Andy Burnham speaks after being confirmed as the Labour Party’s new leader and Britain’s next prime minister, during a conference in central London on 17 July 2026 (AFP)
Off
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) finally ruled last week that the Myanmar government
carried out a genocide
when its army slaughtered thousands of Rohingya Muslims in an orgy of planned killing and mass rape.
This is the second time that the ICJ has found that
genocide
was committed against a Muslim population. Twenty years ago, it reached that verdict in the wake of the
systematic execution
of more than 8,000 Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica.
That could become three times if the ICJ ultimately resolves that
Israel
’s ongoing slaughter of
Palestinians
in Gaza - where
more than 74,000
have been confirmed dead so far, almost all of them Muslim - amounts to a
genocide
.
The world has become an intolerably dangerous place if you are Muslim.
French writer Renaud Camus once warned that Muslim immigration would wipe out white Europeans. “The great replacement is very simple,”
he said in 2012
. “You have one people, and in the space of a generation you have a different people.”
Meanwhile,
China
has held hundreds of thousands of Muslims in secretive
detention camps
in recent years, while the Muslim community in
India
has been denounced
as a “virus”
by the chief minister of Uttar Pradesh.
This view that Islam is a danger to humanity is impossible to substantiate. When Muslims travel to other countries, they normally arrive as victims of oppression, war or civil conflict, not as aggressors.
Yet across much of the globe, Muslims are portrayed as the enemy - and that includes in
Britain
.
Islamophobic tropes
Pick up a newspaper. Read a book on current affairs. Consult a think tank. Listen to a politician. Go down to the pub. You will hear the same story: Islam is on the march, hell-bent on destroying the West.
Muslims are presented as invaders, enemies of civilisation, parasites, unpatriotic - uncomfortably similar to the tropes deployed before the Srebrenica and Myanmar genocides.
According to the British Muslim Trust, there were 78 verified
attacks involving mosques
over the 12 months to July 2026. In recent decades, several Muslims have been murdered simply
for being Muslim
, while others get abused, targeted or beaten up. They fear going out at night.
This past April, a man was
jailed for 13 years
after raping a Sikh woman because he believed she was Muslim.
It is easy to understand why some openly racist politicians dash along to Spectator events - and equally easy to understand why others failed to show
Yet the systematic demonisation of Muslims has become a central part of the narrative of the British political and media classes in the 21st century. As I set out in my book
The Fate of Abraham
, this rhetoric has strong historical roots. But it is now so much a part of normal discussion that almost nobody notices.
At Westminster in particular, there is an adamantine reluctance to challenge the demonisation of a relatively small section of the British population. Politicians are rightly wide awake to the problem of
antisemitism
, a poisonous virus that has been deeply embedded in western Christian DNA for a millennium of British history.
But the majority of British MPs and newspapers flatly refuse to acknowledge that
Islamophobia
has become a problem in contemporary Britain.
Wednesday night provided a powerful and very telling example. Politicians from the main political parties gathered in central London to celebrate the Spectator
Parliamentarian of the Year awards
.
The most senior politicians in Britain were singled out for awards, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch. Former foreign secretary David Lammy and Michael Gove, the former Tory cabinet minister who now edits the Spectator, presented the awards.
On the face of things, this was an admirable cross-party event, when journalists and politicians resolved for an evening to overcome their differences and celebrate the fact that we British have the good fortune to live in a parliamentary democracy. (The revered Spectator political columnist Henry Fairlie once memorably recorded that he slept more soundly in his bed when Parliament was sitting).
Troubling message
But let’s pause a moment and reflect on how all this good cheer and cross-bench jollification looks and feels if you are a British Muslim. This past summer, the Centre for Media Monitoring
produced a report
on the Spectator’s coverage of Islam.
It found that the magazine’s extensive (one might even say obsessive) output on Islam portrays Muslims as invaders who don’t belong in this country, don’t share British values, and threaten our public spaces.
The report also documents how Spectator writers substantiate this thesis through misrepresentations, fabrications, vulgar abuse, and conspiracy theories. Some of the examples are horrifying.
Many observers would regard such coverage as Islamophobic. Not the Spectator, which refuses to frame Islamophobia in its accepted sense as an irrational fear, hatred or prejudice directed at Muslims for being Muslim.
How mainstream media fuels the UK's Islamophobia crisis
Read More »
Instead, it turns the concept on its head, arguing that the term is a cynical attempt to exempt Muslims from criticism, and to import a blasphemy law through the back door.
The magazine ran the headline: “There’s not enough Islamophobia in the Conservative Party.” After an outcry the Spectator changed the headline.
But one only has to imagine the career-ending consequences - not just for the writer, but also the editor, and indeed the magazine itself - that would (rightly) follow if a Labour magazine asserted “there’s not enough antisemitism in Labour”.
Lammy might be interested to learn that the magazine recently
ran two articles
calling for the rehabilitation of the racist 20th-century Tory politician Enoch Powell.
Defenders of the Spectator are entitled to point out that Britain is a free country, and any magazine or newspaper is permitted to propagate whatever views it likes, no matter how bigoted or divisive, so long as they stay within the law.
But that is not the case with political parties. When senior politicians accept awards, they do not send out a message that they agree with the organisers’ beliefs and objectives, and it would be absurd to claim that they do. Yet they are signalling that they regard the Spectator’s commentary on Muslims as within the boundaries of acceptable discourse.
It is easy to understand why some openly racist politicians dash along to Spectator events - and equally easy to understand why others, like Zack Polanski’s Green Party, failed to show.
When Burnham accepted his well-deserved award as politician of the year (last year’s recipient was Reform UK leader Nigel Farage), he was not endorsing the Spectator’s compulsive hostility to Muslims. But he certainly was sending the message that the Spectator operates within the acceptable boundaries of public discourse when it demonises Muslims.
That is a troubling message to send out at any time - all the more so as Islamophobia Awareness Month reaches its climax.

items.title: Israeli group promoting illegal settlements touring UK reported to police over 'threat'
items.content:
Israeli group promoting illegal settlements touring UK reported to police over 'threat'
Submitted by
Imran Mulla
on
Fri, 11/27/2026 - 11:02
Shivat Zion, which promotes West Bank settlements, allegedly threatened Palestinian rector of Glasgow University
Ghassan Abu-Sittah, the rector of Glasgow University, pictured in 2024 (Henry Nicholls/AFP)
Off
An
Israeli
non-profit organisation promoting illegal settlements in occupied
Palestinian
territory that is touring
Britain
has been reported to the police over an alleged threat to the Palestinian rector of Glasgow University, Dr Ghassan Abu-Sittah.
Abu-Sittah, a British Palestinian surgeon who operated in Gaza during Israel's genocide and the rector of Glasgow University, had last week
criticised
Shivat Zion and the "failure of the British government to move against these companies, that are basically facilitating the commission of crimes".
In a
statement
to the National newspaper earlier this week Shraga Evers, a senior Shivat Zion official, responded by saying: "Honestly, I don’t care what Sheikh Ghassan Abu-Sittah says; he is a Hamas supporter - it’s like asking me about a statement by a staunch Adolf Hitler fan about Jews.
"I would like to send him our regards in his own language: كُلّ كَلْب بِيجِي يُومُه [every dog has its day]. Nazi and Hamas ideology isn’t distant from each other with regards to Jews."
The Arabic phrase "every dog has its day" was used by Israeli officials in relation to Yahya Sinwar, the Hamas leader in Gaza whom Israel killed in 2024. Shivat Zion works with the Israeli Ministry of Aliyah and Integration, and says on its
website
: "We’re here to help with your Aliyah and Integration into Israeli life!"
Last week MEE
reported
that a page on Shivat Zion's website
promotes
a kibbutz in Gush Etzion, a collection of settlements in the illegally
occupied
West Bank, while other pages promoted events and teacher training in illegal Israeli settlements.
Shivat Zion's two-week tour began last Sunday with an event in Glasgow and is continuing in cities across Britain.
MEE has approached Shivat Zion for comment.
'Incitement to violence'
Abu-Sittah
responded
by calling Evers' remarks "incitement to violence", adding: "If this was a country with a functioning police force, that didn't spend its time arresting thousands of pensioners because they held up a placard, then this man would be arrested."
Evers has
said
he lives in Efrat, an illegal West Bank settlement. He is currently touring the UK with Shivat Zion.
MEE understands that Jewish Anti-Zionist Action (Jaza), a British activist group, has reported Shivat Zion and Evers to Police Scotland.
Talia Woodin, a spokesperson for Jaza, said: "Shivat Zion is so confident sending a racist, violent diatribe to a newspaper because of the impunity it feels, bolstered by the Israeli state’s support for pro-settlement groups."
Woodin added: "Making a death threat against a heroic British Palestinian doctor and elected university official is utterly deplorable and must now be the last straw. This extremist group must be sanctioned and banned from operating in the UK."
Israeli non-profit helping Britons move to occupied West Bank to tour UK cities
Read More »
Labour MP Abtisam Mohamed
asked
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband "what specific action can be taken against" Shivat Zion during a parliamentary Foreign Affairs Committee hearing earlier this week.
Miliband
said
he would not comment on Shivat Zion specifically, but added: "We do not want to see advertising of settlement property. We do not want to see advertising of those sorts of opportunities."
Pressed on whether action would be taken against Shivat Zion, he responded: "We will ensure we have a comprehensive [sanctions] regime."
In September, the UK government
recognised
Israel's occupation of Palestinian territory as illegal and announced comprehensive sanctions on Israeli settlements.
Implementing the full sanctions could take up to nine months, according to government sources.
Sara Husseini, the director of the British Palestinian Committee, said Shivat Zion spokesperson Evers "has exposed the prejudice and disdain in which they hold Palestinians, underscoring the intent to ethnically cleanse the Palestinian people from our homeland with the full backing and involvement of the Israeli state".
Husseini added: "The UK, particularly in light of its recent announcements on sanctions, should take swift action to ban such organisations from promoting unlawful activities."
MEE has contacted Police Scotland for comment.

items.title: UN urges Costa Rica to let in Palestinians rapporteur
items.content:
The United Nations on Friday urged Costa Rica to urgently reconsider its ban on admitting the UN special rapporteur on Palestinian rights and let her into the country.
Costa Rica's government said Thursday it had denied entry to Francesca Albanese, who has accused Israel of genocide, because she was the subject of an "international alert over links to terrorist acts".
Italian lawyer Albanese is the UN special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Palestinian territory occupied since 1967.

items.title: Trump backs Iraqi leader's efforts to assert more state authority
items.content:
Nov 27 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump on Friday backed the Iraqi leader's drive to assert state control, including stopping the smuggling of Iraqi oil, moves that put Baghdad in direct confrontation with Iran's militia allies and Kurdish authorities.
"We support Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s efforts to assert state authority throughout Iraq, stop the smuggling of Iraqi oil, end corruption, and bring all weapons under the exclusive control of the state," Trump said in a Truth Social post.

items.title: Funding cuts force mass closures of shelters for refugee women, UN says
items.content:
By Emma Farge
GENEVA, Nov 27 (Reuters) - Nearly half of shelters for displaced women and girls across over a dozen countries have closed since the beginning of last year due to funding cuts, leaving them more vulnerable to sexual abuse and violence, the UN refugee agency said on Friday.
These safe spaces help survivors of war orabduction to seek psychological support and other services while protecting them from rape and abuse in camps where ill-lit, crowded conditions canincrease risks.

US President Donald Trump said on Friday that the United States supports Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi's efforts to assert state authority throughout the country, including bringing all arms under its control and stopping the smuggling of Iraqi oil.
“We support Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s efforts to assert state authority throughout Iraq, stop the smuggling of Iraqi oil, end corruption, and bring all weapons under the exclusive control of the state,” Trump said in a Truth Social post.

items.title: In Israel, calls for 'unity' are a code for Jewish tribal supremacy
items.content:
In Israel, calls for 'unity' are a code for Jewish tribal supremacy
Submitted by
Orly Noy
on
Thu, 11/26/2026 - 19:43
The foundation runs deeper than a political consensus among the competing blocs: it concerns which citizens are included when they say 'we'
Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, waves after national election exit polls at his party headquarters in Tel Aviv, Israel, on 28 October 2026 (Shir Torem/Reuters)
Off
The saying “when fascism comes to America, it will be wrapped in a flag and carrying a cross” is commonly attributed to American novelist and playwright Sinclair Lewis.
German writer
Thomas Mann
, himself a Nobel laureate in literature, had a slightly different version: “If ever fascism should come to America, it will come in the name of freedom.”
Former Republican President Ronald Reagan, meanwhile, offered
his own version
: “If fascism ever comes to America, it will come in the name of liberalism.”
Whatever form fascism may take when it arrives in the
US
, one thing can be said with certainty: in
Israel
, it arrived in the name of unity.
It is hard to think of a word in the Hebrew language that has been more shamelessly abused than “unity” by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s inciting, divisive gang.
Take, for example, Elisha Madan, the newly elected Likud MK who has
set up
a “Unity Tent” outside the Knesset. “I intend to sit in the tent day and night, in the cold and rain, to give voice to the many people who keep reaching out to me, yearning for unity,” he declared poetically.
This great champion of unity, it is worth recalling, helped establish the
settlement of Avigail
. He was also
filmed
hurling vile slurs at the late human rights activist Ezra Nawi, who had come to the area to protect
Palestinian
residents from settler violence.
Common ground
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, the man who warned before the election that a left-wing government would pose an
existential threat
to the state of Israel, suddenly remembered after the vote to
reach out
to his “Jewish brothers” with a call for unity.
Amir Ohana - the former Knesset speaker who boycotted the
swearing-in ceremony
of Supreme Court president Yitzhak Amit, and who
refused to allow
bereaved families into the Knesset gallery during a Netanyahu speech about the 7 October attacks, instead having them forcibly removed - also
professes
to see unity as a cherished goal, with the 26th Knesset holding the means to achieve it.
The use of the term 'the people of Israel' is no accident. It is a code word, an effective shortcut for establishing a shared sense of tribal belonging
And this week, comedian Guy Hochman
shoved
a camera rudely into MK Ahmad Tibi’s face, shouting at him: “Ahmad, unity? Unity?” This knight of unity is the same man who found the
genocide
in Gaza
particularly amusing
, and a fitting backdrop for a
stand-up performance
intended to boost the morale of the forces of destruction and annihilation.
He is also the same comedian who attended a left-wing demonstration and
declared
that its participants were “scarier than
Qatar
”. Now, he too wants
unity
.
It is easy to dismiss the unity tantrum gripping Netanyahu’s camp as a cynical ploy, designed to neutralise the meaning of its electoral defeat and spare its members the prospect of being banished to the opposition benches.
But the truth is that it rests on something much deeper, rooted in the anomaly of Israeli politics: a political landscape divided not primarily along ideological lines, but above all, over the question of support for Netanyahu.
Remove Netanyahu himself from the equation, and the common ground between the two blocs is far greater than it might appear; on many issues, their areas of agreement actually outweigh their differences.
A call for unity between two blocs that stood firmly together around the most defining event in Israel’s history since its founding - the
perpetration of genocide
against a besieged and defenceless Palestinian population - is not entirely baseless.
But the foundation of this call for unity runs even deeper than a consensus on any particular policy. It concerns the most instinctive sense of belonging shared by members of both blocs: who they mean when they say “we”.
Dangerous distinction
The Israeli right long ago replaced the concept of “Israeli citizens” with the tribal notion of “the people of Israel” - a term that clearly refers exclusively to the
Jewish collective
. This dangerous substitution is no longer confined to the right.
“The people of Israel cannot trust Netanyahu when he claims his motives are not political … We must not allow him to exploit Israel’s security to disrupt the elections,” Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats,
tweeted
about a month before the election.
The distinction between “the people of Israel” and “Israeli citizens” is anything but semantic. It reflects two fundamentally different conceptions of the Israeli collective, only one of which includes Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Why did Golan choose to invoke “the people of Israel” rather than “Israeli citizens”? Are Arab citizens of Israel not equally affected by security concerns? Do they not flee to bomb shelters - when such shelters are available to them - during wartime?
The use of the term “the people of Israel” is no accident. It is a code word, an effective shortcut for establishing a shared sense of tribal belonging and manufacturing intimacy.
How Israel’s election is further excluding Palestinian citizens from politics
Read More »
When Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot
tells
a former Likud voter, disillusioned with Netanyahu, during an election campaign that “as far as I’m concerned, there is no way the people of Israel will not prevail,” he knows exactly what he is doing: building a sense of tribal intimacy whose boundaries are perfectly clear to both men.
It is within those boundaries that the right is now calling on him to gather under its unity campaign - boundaries that necessarily leave Arabs on the outside.
It is hardly surprising, then, that the Arab parties are the only ones presenting a civic discourse as a substantive alternative to the Jewish tribal discourse embodied in the phrase “the people of Israel”.
Here lies one of the great paradoxes of the Zionist state. Since its founding, Israel has relentlessly sought to sever the connection between Arab citizens and their Palestinian national identity, subjecting them to a process of forced “Israelisation”.
Yet the moment Arab citizens seek to give real substance to the citizenship imposed upon them after the
Nakba
, “the people of Israel” are quick to reclassify them as Palestinians and push them back beyond the boundaries of the Israeli collective. This is the declared position of at least two of the four parties that make up the so-called change bloc.
The choice now facing Eisenkot is not merely between two different governing coalitions. It is a choice between two fundamentally different conceptions of the boundaries of Israeli citizenship: between “the people of Israel” and the citizens of Israel. If he chooses the former, he will become, under cover of the “unity” discourse, a pale appendage of a fully fledged Jewish-supremacist coalition.
If he chooses the latter, he will have to accept Arab citizens as full partners in Israeli citizenship, with an equal and legitimate stake in shaping the country’s character - rather than as people whose struggle is limited to securing whatever crumbs the state is willing to throw their way.

items.content:
Dropping of corruption charges against Israeli PM after unusual intervention could set damaging precedent
The Israeli judges presiding over Benjamin Netanyahu’s corruption trial have called on prosecutors to end proceedings, a highly unusual intervention that leaves the attorney general facing a momentous political decision.
The prime minister
has been charged with bribery, fraud and breach of trust
in three complex and overlapping criminal cases that hinge on his relationship with telecoms magnates and other wealthy businessmen. Ending the trial without a ruling
could set damaging precedents
for media independence and how politicians are held to account.

items.title: For whom the bells troll: French town divided over church’s night-time chimes
items.content:
Long-time residents of La Garnache defeat newer neighbours in latest rural culture clash over ‘sensory heritage’
A ding-dong has divided the town of La Garnache in western France over attempts to silence the bells of the local church, which strike all night.
Since 1942, the clock tower of Notre Dame de l’Assomption has chimed an 8th-century hymn every 15 minutes … day and night. Between 10pm and 7am, the bells ring 37 times, adding up to more than 700 individual chimes.

items.title: Under-attack Palestinians find unlikely ally in Israeli retired general
items.content:
The four Israeli soldiers stepped out of their car in the occupied West Bank, their faces masked, their uniforms unmarked and automatic weapons strapped across their shoulders.
They had entered a Palestinian olive grove but, little did they expect, the person there planning to tell them to leave could have once been issuing them orders.
A retired Israeli general, Eyal Ben Reuven, had come that day to the Palestinian town of As Sawiyah, on a mission to prevent some of the rampant violence against Palestinians by extremist Israeli settlers.

items.title: UN warns famine risks rising as hunger hotspots increase
items.content:
By Clara Schoenthaler
ROME, Nov 27 (Reuters) - Hunger is set to worsen significantly in 16 global hotspots over the coming six months, with famine threatening parts of Africa, two United Nations agencies warned on Friday.
The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and World Food Programme (WFP) said Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia, northern Nigeria and Yemen faced the gravest threats, driven by conflict, displacement, economic hardship and extreme weather.

Podcast: are resignations next?
Labour’s internal divisions over the giant Rosebank oilfield have spilled into the open, with nearly 100 Labour MPs – including a handful of frontbenchers – writing to the prime minister to express their opposition to the project.
Ninety-two backbenchers and at least four frontbenchers have signed a letter to Andy Burnham urging him not to let his ministers approve the scheme for the biggest undeveloped field in UK waters.

items.title: At critical juncture, Friedrich Merz finds Germans’ support for Ukraine wavering
items.content:
German chancellor is on difficult terrain, at home and abroad, as he fights to maintain European backing for Kyiv
The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, is navigating choppy waters both at home and abroad over his insistence that Europe must keep up support – both military and financial – for Ukraine.
At a Brussels summit on Thursday, Merz reiterated his view that all EU member states – pointedly, “not 23 or 24” – should support a €45bn (£38bn) loan for Ukraine for 2027. He has
threatened to veto the bloc’s budget
unless all countries sign up to the loan, a stance that saw him accused of “classic blackmail” by Robert Fico, the populist prime minister of Slovakia. Czechia, Hungary and Bulgaria have also voiced their misgivings, to varying degrees, over Berlin’s dogged position.
